On a day of key injuries in the NFL, from Detroit and-or New England, some points of emphasis never change.
Recycling failed ideas won’t win back old friends for Israel
By Jonathan S. Tobin
(Nov. 16, 2026 / JNS) The U.S.-Israel relationship is at a crossroads. The future of an alliance that is vital to the Jewish state’s survival should be the subject of intense concern for Israelis and those who care about them. But the most important thing they should be currently doing is ignoring most of the advice they are receiving from the “experts” who are telling them how to fix it.
Such advice can be heard in both the United States and Israel. A feature published in The New York Times this past Sunday by David Halbfinger, its Jerusalem bureau chief, and an analysis in Yediot Achronot by prominent commentator Nadav Eyal that was also summarized in a lengthy and widely shared poston X, both put forward similar plans explaining how Israelis might win back the large number of Americans who seem to have turned their backs on them.

Bad ideas come back into fashion

The problem these pieces address is real and something Israel’s leaders must acknowledge. But their suggestions are not a product of contemporary thinking. Instead, they are rooted in nostalgia for a bygone past when the foreign-policy establishment could still pretend that their preferred solutions were considered realistic by those who paid attention to regional events. As such, rather than sage advice, they are a trap that will exacerbate Israel’s dilemma, and only make more bloodshed and war likely instead of peace.

Important in and of themselves, both articles reflect a consensus among the liberal elites that dominate the media, academia and cultural institutions in both countries.

Their prescription for Israelis is simple.

It starts with replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister with a new government, presumably led by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, Gen. Gadi Eisenkot, who has just received a mandate from Israeli President Isaac Herzog to attempt to do that. Halbfinger doesn’t specify who should be part of Eisenkot’s coalition, should the latter be able to form one out of the electoral stalemate produced by the Oct. 27 Israeli election for a new Knesset. By contrast, Eyal believes that such a government must include Arab parties that oppose Israel’s existence.

Both implore Eisenkot to prioritize employing draconian measures to end “settler violence” in Judea and Samaria. That is a narrative about the situation in the territories that is not merely false, but used to discredit Netanyahu, in addition to the hundreds of thousands of Jews who live there and the many more Israelis who support them.

The writers then go on to mandate a massive shift in Israeli security policies that would essentially return the country to the naive moment in 1993, when its government embraced the Oslo Accords. It was at that point that Israelis embarked on an attempt to trade “land for peace” that would end with the creation of a Palestinian Arab state alongside Israel, which would effectively end the conflict.

Forgetting 30 years of history

Both pieces sweep away the history of what followed—history that has shaped a broad consensus of Israeli opinion that rejects a return to the Oslo mindset.

That includes the suicide bombings and ensuing slaughter of more than 1,000 people in Israel during the years of the Second Intifada (2000-05), which was the Palestinian answer to the offer of Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and U.S. President Bill Clinton’s of such a state in the Gaza Strip, a share of Jerusalem and almost all of the so-called “West Bank.” It also means ignoring what happened when Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon withdrew every Israeli soldier, settler and settlement from Gaza in the summer of 2005 and how that led to the creation of a Hamas terror state there.

That epic blunder not only backfired. It set in motion the train of events that led to the events of Oct. 7, 2023, and the orgy of mass murder, torture, rape and kidnapping, as well as the subsequent war that produced the current impasse in the Middle East.

Israelis are urged to forget all of that. And they are told to turn a blind eye to the evidence that shows that the basic premise of “land for peace” was flawed—namely, that the Palestinians and those who seek to enable and encourage them abroad aren’t interested in two states or peace. What they want is Israel’s destruction—something that could only be achieved by the genocide of its population, for which the horror of Oct. 7 was merely the trailer.

In place of common-sense conclusions that Israelis, including many of those who voted for the “anyone-but-Bibi” coalition of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennet and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman, is an agenda of “change” that will require them to imagine a world in which they must stop thinking about defeating enemies like Iran, as well as its Hamas and Hezbollah terrorist proxies, and instead go back to trying to appease them.

The alternative, they are told, is to live in a world in which the Americans will abandon them. It is a world that leads to the end of Jewish sovereignty.

Moreover, they both demand that Israelis not delay abandoning a conviction that regards the conflict as a problem to be managed, rather than solved, because of the lack of a peace partner. They must, in both Halbfinger and Eyal’s versions, essentially surrender their security to the delusions that animate the left-wing J Street lobby. That advocates for overturning the will of the Israeli people as expressed in a quarter century of elections and instead imposes the foreign-policy establishment diktat of territorial surrender. This includes not merely Judea, Samaria and Jerusalem, but also the buffer zones Israel established in Southern Lebanon and Syria in order to prevent future terrorist attacks.

Declining support

Why would Israelis even consider such suicidal and irrational policies? They have already been proven not to advance peace. In fact, all movement in that direction has done is empower and encourage Arab and Islamist forces dedicated to Israel’s elimination and the slaughter of its people.

The answer of the “experts” is that many Americans think it’s a good idea. But that doesn’t make it correct.

It’s entirely true that the political problem Israel and its supporters are facing in the United States is serious—and just got worse with the election of Democratic Party majorities in the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate. They are likely to either attempt to place severe conditions on the alliance or try to blow it up altogether.

It’s also possible that two years from now, the next person elected president of the United States could be either deeply skeptical of the U.S.-Israel relationship or an open opponent of it. That could be the case whether the winner of the 2028 presidential election is either a Democrat or a Republican.

The reality is that support for Israel among Americans has declined since Oct. 7.

Polls had already demonstrated a rapid decline in backing for the Jewish state among Democrats in the decades before that awful day. The embrace of the toxic doctrines of critical race theory, intersectionality and settler-colonialism predisposed those on the left to accept the false notion that Jews and Israel are “white” oppressors, who are always in the wrong, and that Palestinians were “people of color,” who are always in the right, no matter what they did.

That set in motion the astonishing process by which the worst mass slaughter of Jews since the Holocaust was the excuse for an unprecedented surge of antisemitism. This was largely enabled by skewed coverage of the post-Oct. 7 war by journalists who had been indoctrinated in these doctrines, and thus willing to normalize and mainstream blood libels about Israel committing “genocide” in Gaza and being an “apartheid” state.

While Republicans still back Israel by large majorities, they are not unaffected by the same notions that dominate most of the American education system, as well as the media, popular culture and fine arts. That’s why younger Republicans fail to recognize that they, too, are being indoctrinated by anti-American and anti-Western ideas and therefore more likely to be less supportive of Israel than older ones.

Antisemitism isn’t caused by Israeli policies

The answer from the pro-Israel community to all this must involve a greater commitment of resources to efforts to counter the algorithms on social-media platforms that promote blood libels and support for independent media that reject these lies, like JNS.

And it must also be rooted in an acceptance of the fact that the antisemitism at the foundation of critiques of Israel’s efforts to defend itself against a genocidal foe cannot be wished away by changing the behavior of the Jewish state or the Jews as a whole. Jew-hatred is always about the Jew-haters.

In America, that’s why leftists peddle the myth that Israel and Jewish sovereignty are the purest expression of racism and settler-colonialism, and whose destruction will save the whole world. And it also explains why some on the far-right embrace myths about Israelis manipulating America to discard its interests as part of a conspiracy involving the Jeffrey Epstein sexual-misconduct scandal.

Neither left nor right is interested in the facts about the war on Israel and the Jews. What they care about is having a scapegoat on which to focus their fears about what troubles them most about the world or is the explanation for what scares them the most about it.

The myth that Halbfinger and Eyal are most interested in selling the Israelis and their allies is one in which the Jewish state’s problems are solely the product of mean-spirited right-wing attitudes promoted by Netanyahu and his coalition partners. They claim that fair-minded Americans who are shocked by the lies they accept about Israeli behavior in Gaza and the “West Bank” can be persuaded to preserve the alliance. Only if Israelis will reject a belief that they must defend their security and replace it with faith in the delusions about the willingness of the Palestinians and the Muslim world to live in peace with them that led a previous generation of leaders, like Shimon Peres and Barak, to believe in the fairy tale of a new Middle East that would resemble Belgium and the Netherlands.

Appeasement won’t win them back

But does anyone seriously believe that jailing the tiny minority of Jews who might be committing violence in Judea and Samaria in response to the daily toll of Arab terrorism there will fix Israel’s problems with those who believe in such nonsense?

Or that liberal Democrats who fear being primaried by radical Democratic Socialists because of insufficient hostility to Israel will be persuaded to reconstruct the long-gone bipartisan consensus in favor of the Jewish state? Even a government in Jerusalem that would try to revive a two-state solution that Palestinians have no interest in pursuing would ultimately be labeled an “obstacle” to peace by those who refuse to grant the objects of their sympathy any agency for their situation.

Or that those few Republicans, like apparently Vice President JD Vance, who think the antisemitic groyper vote will propel them to power would be happier with an Israeli government that puts its faith in policies designed by J Street? Would they embrace a weak Israel made vulnerable to its foes by concessions that will make it impossible to be the “America First” ally that is an asset rather than a burden to the United States?

There are no easy answers for Israelis as they confront a situation whereby Americans taught to believe that they are evil gain more power. They must instead become more self-reliant, as well as better-equipped to counter the lies spread about them.

What they cannot do is sacrifice their future survival by repeating the mistakes they made during the period when belief in Oslo—and the inevitability of land for peace and a two-state solution—dominated their politics.

Democrats will be more likely to welcome an Israeli prime minister not named Netanyahu to Washington. But in the long run, their caucuses and their base will not be satisfied by Israeli leaders, no matter who they are, if they aren’t willing to surrender their security or their state.

The reality Israelis understand

There is a reason why Eisenkot and his allies didn’t campaign for the policies embraced by J Street. Instead, they focused their efforts on ousting a prime minister who could be accused of being responsible for the Oct. 7 disaster that happened on his watch or on forcing the Haredim to serve in the Israeli military the way other Israeli Jews must. They did so because doing the bidding of those who claim that surrendering rational security policies will win them back American public opinion is rejected by the overwhelming majority of Israelis.

The Israeli people know that returning to efforts to trade land for peace, such as creating a Palestinian state in Judea and Samaria, and making even worse Oct. 7-style atrocities possible, is not so much ill-advised as it is insane. The fact that some misinformed or biased Americans disagree doesn’t change that they are right about this.

Attempting to win back U.S. support by listening to the advice of Halbfinger and Eyal will not just fail as politics. It is a formula for eviscerating the basic premise of the alliance, which rests on Israel’s ability to defend itself and be a vital pro-American force in a region filled with regimes that are neither democratic nor reliable friends of the United States. Moreover, the appeal to the common values rooted in the foundational beliefs of Western civilization that have long united the two peoples will not persuade those Americans, whether on the left or far right, who no longer embrace them.

The only alternative to this bad advice is for Israel—no matter who leads its government—to stay strong, reject suicidal concessions and do a better job of explaining itself to the world. Counseling to wait for a return to sanity in an American public square, where toxic forces have persuaded so many to buy into antisemitic blood libels and myths about Israel, isn’t satisfying to those who demand immediate solutions, even if they will make things worse.

Still, the pendulum of American politics never stops swinging. Those who assume that current intellectual fashions are permanent are always proven incorrect. And that includes those establishment figures who have always been wrong when it comes to their pet solutions to the conflict.

Until public opinion swings back in the direction of support for America’s sole democratic ally in the Middle East—the sole Jewish state on the planet—friends of Israel must continue to fight for the truth and refuse to be intimidated into surrender.

THE PARATROOPERS DROPPED INTO DISASTER

September 24, 1943. The Red Army launched 4,575 paratroopers behind German lines near the Dnieper. Many landed directly among German troops whose arrival Soviet intelligence had failed to detect.

Within hours, the airborne assault had collapsed. Some survivors would fight on for nearly two months.

The disaster was not caused by a single navigational error or an unexpectedly determined German defence. It was the result of an ambitious military plan overtaken by events, inadequate reconnaissance, unreliable transport arrangements and a command structure that committed its soldiers before the preparations necessary for success had been completed.

Yet what happened after the landing also deserves attention. The scattered paratroopers did not all perish in the initial fighting. Some reorganized in the forests of occupied Ukraine, disrupted German communications and eventually returned to Soviet lines after weeks of fighting behind the enemy.

Their story reveals both the remarkable endurance of Soviet soldiers and the terrible consequences of failures at higher levels of command.

The Strategic Opportunity

In September 1943, Germany's position on the Eastern Front was deteriorating rapidly. The German offensive at Kursk had failed in July, and the Soviet counteroffensives that followed had recaptured Oryol, Belgorod and Kharkiv. German formations were retreating westwards across Ukraine, abandoning territory in the hope of establishing a defensible position along the Dnieper River.

The river presented a formidable obstacle. Wide stretches of water, difficult approaches and high ground on the western bank offered defenders significant advantages. German commanders hoped the Dnieper would form the central obstacle in a broader defensive system often called the Eastern Wall.

The Soviet leadership was determined to prevent that line from becoming secure.

General Nikolai Vatutin's Voronezh Front advanced towards the Dnieper south of Kyiv, with Lieutenant-General Pavel Rybalko's 3rd Guards Tank Army leading the pursuit. By September 22, Soviet advance detachments had crossed the river near the Bukryn bend and secured several small footholds on its western bank.

These bridgeheads presented both an opportunity and a problem. Infantry could cross using small boats and improvised equipment, but establishing a sustainable offensive position required engineers, artillery, tanks, ammunition and supplies. The Germans could move reinforcements along roads on the western bank faster than Soviet forces could transport heavy equipment across the river.

The Soviet command therefore proposed an airborne operation to disrupt the German rear. Paratroopers would seize important terrain, interfere with reinforcements and help the ground armies transform their vulnerable footholds into a major bridgehead.

The concept was consistent with Soviet ideas of deep battle, which envisaged striking an enemy's communications and reserves while frontline forces attacked the main defensive position.

But doctrine alone could not overcome the practical requirements of an airborne operation.

For the wider Dnieper campaign, including bridgeheads, dated maps and the battle for control of the crossings, see Ostkrieg's historical study:

https://t.co/DO6v1k9si9

An Ambitious Plan with Too Many Assumptions

The Soviets assembled a provisional airborne corps of approximately 10,000 men under Major-General Ivan Zatevakhin. It comprised the 1st, 3rd and 5th Guards Airborne Brigades, whose soldiers had been trained to land behind German lines and operate independently until ground forces could reach them.

The original plan included successive parachute landings, gliders carrying artillery, aerial reconnaissance, bombardment of German positions, air support after landing and continued deliveries of food and ammunition. Communications teams and artillery observers were supposed to accompany the airborne force, allowing its commanders to coordinate with Soviet armies on the eastern bank.

These arrangements suggest that the planners understood the requirements of such an operation. The failure lay in their inability to deliver them.

The front was moving rapidly, and railway shortages prevented troops and equipment from reaching their departure airfields according to schedule. Bad weather disrupted aircraft movements and aerial reconnaissance. By September 23, the Soviet command was forced to postpone the drop by twenty-four hours and alter the composition of the initial force.

Only the 3rd and 5th Guards Airborne Brigades would make the first landing. The 1st Brigade was held back, with the possibility of joining the operation later.

The revised orders reached subordinate commanders dangerously late.

Historian David Glantz records that brigade commanders received their final instructions roughly ninety minutes before loading, while company commanders had only fifteen minutes to explain their missions. Some platoon leaders were still briefing their soldiers aboard the aircraft.

Such delays mattered enormously. An airborne force could not simply land and begin fighting as an intact formation. Its men first had to locate their assembly areas, recover weapons, identify neighbouring units and determine where the enemy was positioned. These tasks were complicated even under favourable circumstances, and they became nearly impossible when soldiers had been given inadequate time to understand their objectives.

Worse still, the German army had been moving into the intended landing areas while the Soviets were completing their preparations.

The Enemy Was Already There

The German XXIV Panzer Corps had withdrawn towards the Dnieper and moved formations into defensive positions near Kaniv. By September 24, several of its divisions were occupying the area, while the 19th Panzer Division was moving towards the same sector from the Kyiv direction.

These movements transformed the situation on the western bank.

What had recently been a comparatively weakly defended area was becoming a concentration of experienced German infantry, armoured troops and supporting weapons. Instead of landing behind a thin defensive screen, the Soviet paratroopers were approaching positions occupied by forces already preparing to resist a Soviet breakthrough.

The Soviet command did not have an accurate picture of the enemy's deployment. Bad weather had prevented adequate aerial reconnaissance, and the speed of the German withdrawal meant that earlier intelligence was becoming obsolete.

The twenty-four-hour postponement, intended to address Soviet logistical difficulties, had also given German formations more time to occupy the intended landing zones.

This was the decisive intelligence failure. The entire operation depended upon assumptions about the enemy's location that were no longer valid, yet the assault proceeded.

September 24: The Landings Begin

The first aircraft carrying the 3rd Guards Airborne Brigade departed at approximately 18:30 on September 24. Aircraft carrying elements of the 5th Brigade followed later that evening.

Even before the paratroopers reached the river, the operation's transport arrangements began to unravel.

Aircraft had not assembled in sufficient numbers, pilots refused to carry the loads originally assigned to them, and inadequate refuelling facilities disrupted the carefully planned departure sequence. Soldiers and equipment were reassigned at short notice, with some men moving between aircraft in the hope of joining an earlier flight.

The consequences were substantial.

Of approximately 500 planned sorties, only 298 were flown. A total of 4,575 paratroopers reached the landing operation, accompanied by 660 light parachute bags containing ammunition and supplies. Another 2,017 men remained at the departure airfields.

The aircraft intended to deliver the 3rd Brigade's 45-millimetre antitank guns did not arrive in time. For soldiers who were about to encounter German armour, this omission would prove particularly serious.

The approaching aircraft then came under German antiaircraft fire.

Pilots manoeuvred to avoid the incoming fire, often flying at high speeds and altitudes that made accurate parachute drops extremely difficult. The absence of effective ground markers further complicated navigation.

The planned landing area measured approximately ten by fourteen kilometres. Instead, the troops were scattered across a region approximately thirty by ninety kilometres.

Some aircraft dropped their passengers east of the Dnieper among Soviet forces. Others released men into the river itself. Thirteen aircraft returned without dropping their passengers at all.

The most unfortunate soldiers descended directly into German positions.

Accounts from the 19th Panzer Division describe Soviet aircraft arriving over the village of Dubari just as German armoured and motorized troops were moving through the area. German soldiers opened fire on the descending paratroopers with rifles, machine guns and antiaircraft weapons.

Other Soviet groups landed among German supply columns, maintenance detachments and infantry formations. Some reached the ground only to discover that their designated assembly areas were already occupied.

The force had lost its concentration before the survivors could begin the mission for which they had trained.

From Airborne Assault to Scattered Resistance

The experience of a Soviet paratrooper landing near Kaniv varied enormously depending upon where his aircraft released him. A man who reached a wooded area with his equipment might have some chance of finding other survivors. A soldier who landed among German armoured vehicles or in an open field near a defensive position faced a very different prospect.

The original plan assumed that soldiers would gather into organized units, establish communications and move against assigned objectives. The scattered landings made those arrangements largely impossible.

Radios were lost, damaged or separated from the men responsible for operating them. Only five of the twenty-six radio sets carried by the force were initially functioning. Without communications, isolated groups could not determine where neighbouring units had landed, request reinforcements or coordinate with the Soviet armies attempting to cross the river.

German forces began systematic searches of the countryside on September 25. The white parachutes scattered across the landscape helped reveal the location of landings, while German patrols captured or destroyed much of the equipment dropped with the soldiers.

The results were devastating.

German accounts recorded hundreds of Soviet dead and prisoners within particular sectors during the first twenty-four hours. These figures describe local engagements rather than the complete losses of the operation, and German claims of having eliminated the airborne threat must be treated cautiously.

They nevertheless reveal how quickly the Soviet assault had deteriorated.

Within days, the Germans considered the immediate threat largely contained. The survivors were too dispersed to threaten the defensive line in the manner Soviet planners had intended.

For the Red Army, the mission of seizing and holding important terrain behind the river had become impossible. The soldiers still in German-held territory were now fighting primarily to survive, reassemble and recover whatever supplies they could find.

Between September 25 and October 5, Soviet records identified forty-three separate groups containing approximately 2,300 men from the original landing force. Other soldiers had been killed, captured or isolated, while some had joined partisan detachments.

The survivors were fighting a war without the organization their commanders had intended to provide.

The Forests Around Kaniv

The terrain of central Ukraine became one of the most important factors determining the fate of the scattered soldiers.

In the northern landing areas, more open countryside and substantial German defensive positions made concealment difficult. Small groups moved independently, avoiding patrols and attempting to reach safer ground.

Farther south, wooded terrain provided better opportunities to assemble. In the forests around Kaniv, Lieutenant-Colonel Pavel Sidorchuk, commander of the 5th Guards Airborne Brigade, began gathering soldiers from different units.

By October 5, Sidorchuk had assembled approximately 600 men. The following day, a radio crew joined his formation and succeeded in establishing contact with Soviet headquarters. This communication link eventually permitted aircraft to deliver ammunition and other supplies, allowing the growing force to conduct more organized operations.

Sidorchuk's command gradually developed into a substantial fighting formation. It included infantry battalions, reconnaissance personnel, engineers and other specialists recovered from the original landing force.

The men no longer attempted to carry out the September mission. Instead, they attacked German installations, interfered with communications and gathered intelligence for the advancing Soviet armies.

Their activities also brought them into contact with partisan formations operating in occupied Ukraine. These groups had their own experience of German security operations and the difficult conditions of warfare behind the front.

On October 19, Sidorchuk moved his men towards the Tagancha forest, where another group of survivors joined them. The force now numbered more than 1,000 soldiers.

Three days later, on October 22, they struck the railway between Korsun and Tagancha station and destroyed a train. They subsequently attacked German positions and supply installations around Buda-Vorobievska and Potashnya.

The Germans responded with attacks on the Soviet forest positions, inflicting losses and forcing Sidorchuk to withdraw farther south.

By late October, however, the surviving brigade had grown to approximately 1,200 men. It continued conducting raids and reconnaissance, while its communications with Soviet headquarters provided a means of directing useful intelligence towards the advancing armies.

This was a considerable achievement by troops who had been scattered, isolated and badly supplied for weeks.

It was not, however, a reversal of the original failure. The September operation had not secured its intended defensive lines, and German reinforcements had not been prevented from containing the Bukryn bridgeheads.

The surviving force had adapted to a disaster rather than fulfilled the mission that produced it.

November 13: Another Attempt to Help the River Crossing

By November, Soviet forces were preparing further crossings of the Dnieper near Cherkasy. Sidorchuk's brigade, still operating in the German rear, established contact with the Soviet 52nd Army and received new orders.

The paratroopers were to attack German positions around Lozovok, Sekirna and Svidovok, capturing the settlements and supporting a crossing by the 254th Rifle Division.

This time, the surviving airborne troops were not expected to secure an extensive region independently. Their task was narrower: attack German positions from behind at the same time that Soviet ground forces crossed the river.

During the early hours of November 13, the paratroopers advanced against the villages. Fighting developed around Svidovok, where German strongpoints were supported by tanks. Soviet troops used infantry weapons, antitank rifles and surprise to overcome parts of the German defence.

Other detachments captured positions near Lozovok and Sekirna.

Yet the operation again encountered a serious coordination failure. The 254th Rifle Division was unable to make its planned crossing during the night, leaving Sidorchuk's men exposed to German counterattacks.

German reinforcements, supported by additional tanks, attacked Svidovok and forced the paratroopers to withdraw into the forests rather than risk encirclement.

The immediate tactical operation had not unfolded as intended, but the Soviet ground offensive continued.

By November 15, elements of the 254th Rifle Division and 52nd Army had linked up with the airborne survivors. Sidorchuk's brigade remained in combat for almost another two weeks before being withdrawn to the rear.

For men who had originally expected to participate in a relatively brief assault followed by relief from advancing ground forces, their ordeal had lasted approximately two months.

What Did the Operation Actually Achieve?

The September airborne mission was intended to help Soviet forces enlarge their Dnieper bridgeheads by securing terrain behind the German defences and preventing reinforcements from reaching the river.

It did not accomplish those objectives.

The scattered landings prevented the troops from forming the planned defensive perimeter, communications failed, important equipment never reached the battlefield and the German army retained sufficient freedom of action to contain the Bukryn bridgeheads.

Some surviving paratroopers eventually carried out useful raids, destroyed supplies, gathered intelligence and assisted later Soviet river crossings. Those achievements deserve recognition, but they belonged to an improvised campaign conducted after the original operation had effectively collapsed.

Historian David Glantz estimated that more than 60 per cent of the airborne force never returned. The figure should not be interpreted as an exact number of men killed, because the surviving records encompass soldiers who died, were captured, disappeared or remained unaccounted for after dispersal.

The human cost was nevertheless enormous.

The episode also influenced Soviet military practice. The Dnieper landing became the last major operational parachute assault conducted by the Red Army during the Second World War. Airborne troops continued serving throughout the conflict, but Soviet commanders increasingly employed these formations in conventional ground operations rather than repeating large parachute drops behind German lines.

The Red Army ultimately achieved major victories in the wider Dnieper campaign. Kyiv was liberated on November 6, 1943, and Soviet forces established important footholds west of the river that enabled further offensives during the winter.

Yet those victories came through sustained operations involving infantry, armour, engineers, artillery and enormous logistical effort, not through the successful execution of the September parachute assault.

Courage Cannot Repair a Failed Plan

The disaster near the Dnieper illustrates an uncomfortable truth about military history.

A successful campaign can contain catastrophically mismanaged operations, and the courage demonstrated by individual soldiers can coexist with serious failures by the commanders responsible for employing them.

The Soviet airborne troops were not simply inexperienced soldiers who failed to perform their assigned duties. Many were trained men committed to an operation whose essential requirements had not been met. Their commanders lacked reliable information about German deployments, the aircraft schedule had collapsed, and the landing force did not possess adequate heavy weapons or communications.

The decision to proceed transformed those deficiencies into a battlefield disaster.

For the survivors, what followed was a struggle shaped less by doctrine than by the practical requirements of staying alive. They gathered scattered comrades, recovered supplies, fought German patrols and moved through forests that offered protection from an enemy with greater mobility and firepower.

Some eventually became part of a reorganized force capable of conducting substantial attacks. Others were never recovered.

Their story deserves attention not because the initial operation succeeded, but because it failed so badly, and because the men who survived continued fighting long after the plans developed for them had ceased to have any meaning.

The Soviet victory in the Battle of the Dnieper was real, as was its strategic importance to the defeat of Nazi Germany. But so too were the lives lost in an airborne operation whose planners had failed to account for the conditions their soldiers would confront.

The distinction matters. Remembering the achievement of the Red Army does not require excusing the decisions that needlessly increased its losses.

And remembering the paratroopers who fought their way through the forests of Ukraine requires more than celebrating their endurance. It requires asking why so many of them were placed in that position in the first place.

I joined the (less than) 1% of women in the world who have finished a marathon 

This time last year I was overweight and not running at all. I went on a weight loss journey where I lost 50 pounds and fell in love with running in the process. Ive become more disciplined and I love fitness + nutrition. I trained alone 5 days a week for 6 months straight despite my other obligations and committed to sobriety for over a year now.

This marathon was an absolute dog fight for 90% of the race. Everything that could have possibly gone wrong absolutely did. I trained for speed but Im disappointed I never got to use it. My quads and left abductor locked up early on and I never fully recovered for the rest of the race. That never happened to me before so I was troubleshooting the pain and running at the same time but every time I picked up speed it locked back up and I had to stop for aid. I couldnt keep a pacer from all the stopping without being able to sprint back up. My pace alerts on my watch didnt work. My back was bleeding from my running vest being tight where my bra clip was in the wrong place. My headphones randomly died so I was left the with sound of my feet hitting the pavement and the struggle in my breathing for hours as it was 30 degrees and the wind overtook me on the endless rolling hills I was underprepared for. I made the executive decision that I wasnt willing to get injured which led to me finishing at double my usual pace + 2 extra hours on feet. I gave it my best but this is not the best I have to offer and that’s okay. This race taught me so many things I could have only learned through experience. After I recover Im excited to train harder now that I know what to do!

Huge thanks to the spectators who showed OUT with support throughout the city, thats what I’ll remember most about this day. I loved high fiving kids, dancing with DJ’s, and helping out other struggling runners. As a Charlotte native, it was full circle for me to be the first in my bloodline to achieve this in the same streets I grew up in. Thank you to my friends and family for all your encouragement and support!

The end of a thing is a better than the beginning and patience is better than pride

Laurent Nkunda And Bosco Ntaganda, Two Rebel Leaders Who Shaped The History Of The Conflict In Eastern Congo

Two rebel military commanders. Closely connected military careers. One region that has endured years of rebellion, warfare, division and insecurity.

For decades, the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has experienced armed conflicts involving rebel groups, defections from the national army, the interests of neighbouring countries and struggles for political power.

Laurent Nkunda and Bosco Ntaganda were two prominent military commanders who played significant roles in this conflict, particularly through their involvement in the National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP).

LAURENT NKUNDA — LEADER OF THE CNDP

Laurent Nkunda was a former military officer in the Congolese army who later became one of the most prominent rebel leaders in eastern Congo.

In 2006, he helped establish the CNDP and became its leader. The group operated mainly in North Kivu province.

His forces fought against the Congolese government army and were accused of committing serious crimes against civilians, including killings and recruiting children into armed groups.

The CNDP eventually became a major military and political threat to the Congolese government.

In January 2009, Rwandan authorities arrested Nkunda, bringing his leadership of the group to an end.

BOSCO NTAGANDA — THE MILITARY COMMANDER

Bosco Ntaganda first became a senior military commander in the Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) in the Ituri region before later joining Laurent Nkunda’s CNDP in North Kivu.

Within the CNDP, he served as Chief of Staff, playing a significant role in directing the group’s military operations.

Following Laurent Nkunda’s removal from the leadership of the CNDP in 2009, Ntaganda took over the group’s leadership and was subsequently integrated into the Congolese national army with the rank of General.

In 2012, he defected from the Congolese national army and became one of the leading commanders of the M23 rebellion.

In 2019, the International Criminal Court (ICC) found him guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in the Ituri region between 2002 and 2003.

He was sentenced to 30 years in prison. In 2021, the ICC Appeals Chamber upheld his conviction and sentence.

COMPARING THEIR LEADERSHIP AND MILITARY CAREERS

Laurent Nkunda helped establish the CNDP and transform it into a powerful rebel movement, becoming a central figure in the conflict between the group and the Congolese government.

On the other hand, Bosco Ntaganda’s influence extended across several armed groups and military structures, including the CNDP, the Congolese national army and the M23 rebellion.

Their military careers demonstrate how the leadership of armed groups, the failure to properly integrate former combatants into the national army and the lack of accountability for perpetrators of serious crimes contributed to the repeated outbreak of violence in eastern Congo.

AN IMPORTANT QUESTION

Between these two military commanders, who played a more significant role in creating the security crisis in eastern Congo?

Was it Laurent Nkunda, who founded and led the CNDP rebellion?

Or was it Bosco Ntaganda, who played a major role in the CNDP, joined the Congolese national army and later became one of the leading commanders of the M23 rebellion?

Whose military history had the greatest consequences for the security and stability of the region?

Syria – Saudi Arabia and Yemen: Cooperation Without a Confirmed Deployment 
Saudi–Syrian defence cooperation is established; a Syrian expeditionary deployment to Yemen is not established by the verified official record.
The agreements signed in Riyadh on 4 November demonstrate a substantial bilateral rapprochement, including military cooperation and development financing.
On 9 November, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani denied that Syrian troops were in Yemen or that an imminent deployment was planned.
On 12 November, Yemen’s chargé d’affaires in Damascus also challenged accounts of a deployment arrangement.
Saudi Arabia’s broader coalition-building is more firmly documented: Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have announced measures to implement their collective-defence commitments.
British operational support is independently documented, but European maritime protection, Saudi territorial defence and ground combat in Yemen remain distinct missions.
The principal decision threshold is a documented change in mission, command arrangements and territorial employment—not the announcement of another cooperation agreement. https://t.co/3e32kfjALv

Syria’s Saudi Partnership Must Build Capacity Before It Exports Force
Saudi Arabia’s defence partnership with Syria creates a decision that neither a signing ceremony nor a projected troop total can resolve: whether Damascus can contribute to regional security without exporting the institutional capacity it needs for reconstruction. The agreements signed on 4 November 2026 establish military cooperation; they do not establish an authorised Syrian combat deployment to Yemen. For Riyadh, the attraction is another potential source of assistance. For Damascus, the constraint is a recovery programme requiring security, engineering, procurement and administrative resources at home. European governments face the same distinction from the opposite direction: protecting Saudi territory and commercial navigation does not amount to approving a Syrian land campaign. The governing test is whether cooperation leaves Syria with stronger institutions or a larger inventory of external obligations.
A defence agreement cannot supply an expeditionary army
On 9 November 2026, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani denied that Syrian troops were in Yemen or that a deployment was planned in the near future. On 12 November, Yemen’s chargé d’affaires in Damascus, Mohammed Azzi Baakr, challenged accounts of a deployment arrangement. These are attributable official positions, not independent inspections. They nevertheless prevent a combat intervention from being treated as an acknowledged government decision. The military question begins where the 4 November agreement’s public description ends: which formation, under whose command, supported by which resources, and for how long?
The NATO logistics framework identifies supply, movement, maintenance and supporting services as connected requirements. Its relevance is institutional, not evidence of NATO involvement in Syrian planning. Individual battlefield experience cannot establish collective readiness, equipment availability or endurance. Saudi provision of transport, accommodation or medical services could reduce Damascus’s immediate burden if agreed, but would also make the contribution dependent on those arrangements. A force whose initial movement is funded has not thereby acquired the replacements, maintenance and command capacity required for a continuing mission.

The financing figures measure different claims on the state
The World Bank’s October 2025 assessment of damage during 2011–2024 estimated physical reconstruction costs at US$216 billion, within a US$140–345 billion range. Direct physical damage was estimated separately at US$108 billion; the two measures are not additive. Against that historical requirement, the six Saudi concessional loan agreements signed on 4 November 2026 exceed US$403 million. They are targeted commitments, not verified disbursements or a measure of remaining national reconstruction needs. The EU’s Council background brief of 13 November also identifies a €620 million Syria support package for 2026–2027. None of these figures establishes a fungible budget from which an overseas campaign can be priced.

The Saudi allocations reveal the competing requirements: US$105 million for emergency services, US$100 million for healthcare, US$90 million for Aleppo thermal generation, US$60 million for housing, US$30 million for water metering and more than US$18 million for government financial services. Germany’s ASPIDES application, meanwhile, estimates €18.9 million in additional deployment expenditure for 1 November 2026–31 October 2027. That national military estimate cannot be combined with Syrian development loans or EU assistance. Its significance is the discipline it illustrates: an external commitment needs a defined period, a resource provision and a clear distinction between estimated expenditure and money spent.
Electricity procurement exposes the real capacity constraint

The World Bank’s Syria Electricity Emergency Project shows how financing becomes dependent on institutional execution. The US$146 million grant announced in June 2025 covered transmission, substations and implementation support. The June 2026 mission record subsequently identified clearance, procurement, engineering supervision and security arrangements involving Syria’s Ministries of Defence and Interior. Restoring electricity therefore requires more than generating equipment: sites and access routes must be usable, contracts administered and the network capable of delivering power. These functions are part of the recovery programme’s productive capacity.

The same World Bank mission record states that the transmission-line procurement package excluded the Türkiye connection at that stage and proceeded with the Jordan line. An announced design had already become a more specific implementation decision. That distinction should govern military cooperation as well. Under the Saudi programme, rehabilitation of generating units in Aleppo will produce its intended service benefit only where the wider system permits delivery. If an external mission draws on personnel needed for domestic engineering, coordination or security, its opportunity cost would appear partly in delayed services. The record does not quantify that displacement; a competent decision must establish whether it exists before accepting another continuing obligation.
Domestic approval and territorial authority remain separate

Syria’s Constitutional Declaration of 13 March 2025 distributes relevant powers rather than creating one unlimited deployment authority. Article 30 assigns treaty ratification and budget approval to the People’s Assembly; Article 32 identifies the president as supreme commander; Article 37 concerns final treaty signature; and Article 41 addresses mobilisation and war following National Security Council approval. Their application depends on the actual instrument and mission. A training assignment should not automatically be treated as a declaration of war, but presidential attendance at a ceremony cannot establish every approval required for sustained combat.

International authority requires a separate assessment. In its 1986 Nicaragua judgment, the International Court of Justice addressed the victim-state request, necessity and proportionality relevant to collective self-defence. Its 2005 Armed Activities judgment emphasised the limits of territorial consent. Applied here, Saudi permission for personnel to operate in Saudi Arabia cannot itself establish Yemeni permission for their presence in Yemen. Security Council Resolution 2216 records the historical Yemeni request for assistance in 2015; that record does not, by itself, establish the current scope of consent for a new Syrian mission. An alliance can organise assistance, but cannot replace these inquiries.
European solidarity is not a common operational mandate

Italy’s existing exposure demonstrates why additional assistance requires a specific decision. In the parliamentary hearing of 8 October 2026, Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto reported 407 personnel in the Saudi presence and distinguished existing arrangements from a possible ad hoc mission requiring parliamentary consideration. France’s 9 November diplomatic statement expressed solidarity with Saudi territorial defence. The UK parliamentary answer of 13 November confirmed counter-air and refuelling operations since 20 October. These records establish different commitments; none establishes approval of a Syrian ground intervention.

Germany’s Bundestag authorised continued ASPIDES participation through 31 October 2027, while the EU operation’s separately established mandate runs to 28 February 2027. Those dates cannot be treated as one automatic commitment. The Council’s March 2026 maritime amendments also added infrastructure-information and capacity-building functions within available means and capabilities. For European governments, the practical choice is whether requested support improves a defined protective function and remains within the relevant authority. General concern about trade and energy disruption cannot establish that an unspecified land campaign would restore commercial passage.
The next two years will charge for obligations left undefined

Over the next 12–24 months, the EU’s 2026–2027 assistance programme and Germany’s nationally authorised ASPIDES period provide concrete intervals for scrutiny. Damascus and Riyadh should measure cooperation through functioning institutions, supportable assignments and completed objectives. European governments should identify any assistance connected to a Syrian mission through its actual function, authority and resource cost. Failure to do so would allow successive renewals and additional tasks to determine the commitment before institutions have assessed its cumulative burden.

The UN Humanitarian Coordinator’s 20 October 2026 statement on Taiz identifies who already bears the consequences when security and services deteriorate: households facing food and fuel prices that had more than doubled, and a city whose water production had halved. Those observations do not establish what a Syrian intervention would change. They establish why force size is an inadequate measure of policy. If the 4 November partnership creates obligations without maintainable capacity or measurable protective results, Syrian service users would bear any domestic displacement, contributing governments would carry continuing support costs, and Yemeni civilians and commercial shipping would remain exposed to an unresolved conflict.

Hand to heart, beloved brothers and sisters of the Blue-White Rose. 

Among the quietest and most intimate capacities of the clearer band are those that arrive through the ancient gateways of smell and taste. Clairalience is the sudden perception of scents where no physical source exists in the room. Clairgustance is the distinct perception of tastes when no physical substance rests upon the tongue. Both frequently appear without warning, linger for only a brief breath, and carry deep memory or quiet presence far more directly than any spoken narrative ever could.

Many individuals experience these fleeting impressions across their lives and quietly set them aside as odd neurological glitches or tricks of the imagination. Yet, in the ancient remembrance of the chambers, they are simply further examples of the biological brain translating non-local or residual data into the familiar sensory formats it already trusts. What follows is the gentle nature of these twin capacities, offered humbly so the sudden fragrance of jasmine in a closed room, the unaccountable metallic note, or the flavor that matches nothing in the mouth can be recognized cleanly, without fear or theatrical inflation.

🌺 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗩𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗹 𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗧𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲

Olfaction and gustation are our oldest, most deeply rooted limbic senses. Unlike sight or hearing, which must pass through layers of analytical sorting and mental labeling, scent and taste connect directly to the primal memory and emotional centers of the human vessel.

When a non-local signal, a seed memory, or a residual environmental field needs to be clothed quickly so the nervous system can register it without shock, the brain frequently selects these ancient channels. They already know how to evoke instant recognition without requiring a long, exhausting explanation. A single phantom scent can deliver an entire atmosphere in one inhalation. A fleeting taste can confirm a quiet presence or a distant timeline resonance with a single, unmistakable note. The translation is remarkably efficient, and often startling precisely because it bypasses our heavier analytical filters.

“Words must knock at the outer gate of the mind and wait to be questioned, yet a single breath of cedar or myrrh walks straight into the heart of the sanctuary and awakens what slept for a thousand years.”

🌬️ 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲: 𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗣𝗵𝘆𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲

The classic experience of clairalience is the sudden, unmistakable aroma of flowers, woodsmoke, familiar perfume, damp earth, or temple incense arising in a space where no physical source exists. The sweet scent of jasmine blooming in the middle of a closed winter room, the warm odor of pipe tobacco where no one has smoked for decades, or the crisp smell of rain on hot stone inside a dry building, these are common, ordinary reports of a thinned filter.

These fleeting scents are most often tied to one of four quiet sources:

𝗔 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗱𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: The lingering atmospheric imprint of an activity, offering, or daily habit once repeated within those walls.

𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: The passing thought or quiet presence of a loved one, living or departed, strongly associated with that specific aroma.

𝗦𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗼𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗽𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲: A brief harmonic overlap with another layer of your own journey where that fragrance was part of your daily landscape.

𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗰𝘁: A gentle, non-verbal acknowledgment that a subtler field has brushed peacefully against your own.

ACC coaching hot seats: O'Brien faces greatest pressure as Key earns relief and Swinney's scrutiny intensifies

Boston College's Bill O'Brien enters the closing stretch of the 2026 football season atop these ACC coaching hot-seat rankings, while Georgia Tech's Brent Key has earned some breathing room and Clemson's Dabo Swinney faces renewed questions following the same game.

Georgia Tech's 20-6 victory at Clemson on November 14 illustrated how quickly the pressure can shift. Key's team responded after a staff shakeup and four consecutive losses. Swinney's team suffered another damaging home defeat, failing to score a touchdown against an opponent that arrived with two victories. Meanwhile, Boston College's 41-7 loss at Notre Dame left the Eagles needing consecutive victories to reach six wins. 

The conference has already seen two coaching changes. NC State dismissed Dave Doeren on October 24, and Florida State dismissed Mike Norvell on November 1. Todd Goebbel and Rick Stockstill, respectively, are included here as the current interim coaches; their predecessors' departures are addressed separately below. 

These rankings are an editorial assessment of job pressure, not a prediction that every highly ranked coach will be fired. Results matter, but so do expectations, tenure, leadership support, contractual protection and evidence of improvement.

Interim coaches require an additional distinction: their uncertainty concerns whether they will receive the permanent appointment. Their placements are provisional judgments about that uncertainty, rather than an assertion that they caused the problems they inherited.

The complete rankings

Assessment: The strongest case for a critical finish among the remaining permanent coaches.

O'Brien's position reflects the combination of last season's collapse and this season's incomplete recovery. Boston College went 7-6 in his first year and 2-10 in his second. Four victories in 2026 represent improvement, but the Eagles have yet to establish that the program has recovered sufficiently. 

The Notre Dame defeat added another difficult performance. Boston College produced only 51 passing yards, and its lone touchdown followed an interception that created a short field. The Eagles' official report identified Syracuse as their next opponent. 

Our assessment: O'Brien needs the finish to demonstrate something tangible: bowl eligibility, competitive offense and evidence that the program's increased expectations are attainable. A loss to a strong Notre Dame team alone would not justify this placement. The broader trajectory does.

He ranks first because the remaining games can materially change the evaluation of his third season. That is different from having verified evidence that Boston College has decided to replace him.

2. Brent Key, Georgia Tech

Assessment: Still under significant pressure, but the Clemson victory provides meaningful relief.

Key's season reached a crisis point before the Clemson trip. Georgia Tech dismissed four assistants on November 9 following its 2-7 start. That was a substantial acknowledgment that the existing operation was failing. 

The response was persuasive. Winning 20-6 at Clemson gave the Yellow Jackets their first victory there since 2008 and showed that the team could respond to disruption with a disciplined performance. 

Contractual protection also matters. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that Key's agreement runs through 2030 and estimated a termination obligation of $18.45 million under its stated year-end assumptions. 

Our assessment: One victory cannot repair a seven-loss season, but it can change the discussion from whether the team has stopped responding to whether the changes offer a credible route forward.

Key remains second because the overall disappointment is substantial. His circumstances, however, improved during the latest weekend. Another competitive showing would strengthen the argument for allowing him to complete the repair.

3. Dabo Swinney, Clemson

Assessment: Mounting performance scrutiny, tempered by an unusually strong résumé and expensive contract.

Clemson's latest defeat was particularly damaging because Georgia Tech entered with a losing record and a reshuffled staff. Swinney acknowledged the frustration afterward.

"Yeah, I'm just sorry," he said, accepting responsibility for the disappointment. 

There is relevant context. Starting quarterback Tait Reynolds left early, and Clemson used multiple quarterbacks. Nevertheless, the loss ended the Tigers' 38-game winning streak against opponents that had losing records at kickoff. 

Swinney's contractual protection is substantial: the published term sheet lists a $57 million university termination payment for 2026. 

Our assessment: Swinney can face more public criticism than coaches above him while still being harder to dismiss. His ranking reflects the widening gap between Clemson's expectations and its current performance.

The remaining games must provide evidence that the program can regain offensive effectiveness and consistency. His achievements remain a powerful consideration, but they do not eliminate scrutiny of the present team.

4. Bill Belichick, North Carolina

Assessment: The finish matters, with university leadership reserving its evaluation until after the season.

UNC's 16-14 loss to Louisville left the Tar Heels 5-5. Carolina remained competitive, but another close home defeat delayed bowl eligibility. The official game center recorded a narrow yardage difference-302 for Louisville and 293 for UNC-illustrating how little separated the teams. 

The most useful job-security evidence came before that game. Chancellor Lee Roberts told WRAL:

"We continue to strongly support the football program and, obviously, evaluate how things have gone at the end of the season, not in the middle of the season."

WRAL also reported that Belichick's contract guarantees compensation through 2027, with no guarantees for the final two seasons.

Our assessment: That statement supports continued evaluation rather than an imminent decision. It also makes the closing games consequential.

Belichick's team has an opportunity to finish with a winning regular season. Doing so would offer a more persuasive case for progress than another season ending without a bowl appearance.

5. Todd Goebbel, NC State - interim

Assessment: High uncertainty about the permanent appointment; limited responsibility for the inherited situation.

Goebbel took over after NC State dismissed Doeren and announced an immediate national search. The university's announcement designated him interim coach for the remainder of the season. 

His first three games produced a victory over California followed by defeats against Duke and Syracuse. The latest loss was especially difficult: NC State led Syracuse 28-13 after three quarters but surrendered 21 fourth-quarter points in a 34-31 defeat. 

Our assessment: Goebbel's placement reflects the uncertainty of continuing as head coach beyond the interim assignment. It should not be read as equivalent to a permanent coach exhausting years of institutional patience.

The closing games offer an opportunity to show organization, player commitment and improved execution under pressure. Those qualities can strengthen his candidacy or professional standing even if the university ultimately selects an outside coach.

His immediate task remains giving the current players a credible chance to finish successfully.

6. Tony Elliott, Virginia

Assessment: A disappointing follow-up season, with substantial reasons for institutional patience.

Virginia's 36-7 victory over California was an important interruption of a three-game losing streak. It moved the Cavaliers to 5-5 and within one victory of bowl eligibility. Two interception returns for touchdowns helped produce Elliott's largest ACC victory margin at Virginia. 

His employment position also requires acknowledging recent success. Virginia announced an extension through the 2030 season in April after Elliott led the program to a school-record 11 victories in 2025. 

Our assessment: Those facts argue against portraying Elliott as a likely dismissal. The concern is whether this season represents a manageable regression or exposes weaknesses that require significant correction.

Another bowl appearance would help establish continuity after last year's breakthrough. Missing the postseason would make the contrast sharper.

His numerical rise from seventh to sixth is principally a consequence of changes elsewhere in the rankings. The latest result improved his position within Virginia's season rather than making it worse.

7. Tosh Lupoi, California

Assessment: Results demand correction, but first-year status materially reduces immediate risk.

California's 36-7 defeat at Virginia left the Bears 3-7. The loss included two Virginia interception returns for touchdowns, turning offensive mistakes into an overwhelming scoring disadvantage.
Lupoi is completing his first season as a college head coach. California appointed him in December 2025, presenting the former Bears player and assistant as the leader of a new phase for the program.

Our assessment: A poor debut deserves scrutiny, particularly when November performances remain uncompetitive. It does not automatically justify assuming the school will abandon a newly installed coach.

The distinction is between a hot seat and pressure to demonstrate a workable plan. Lupoi faces the latter more clearly than the former.

The closing stretch should be evaluated for execution, competitiveness and signs that the roster is improving. Those indicators will shape expectations for 2027, when first-year explanations will carry less weight.

8. Pat Narduzzi, Pitt

Assessment: Moderate pressure to produce a stronger finish.

Pitt's 16-10 home loss to Florida State left the Panthers 6-4 overall and 3-4 in ACC play. Florida State's defense repeatedly stopped late possessions, including a final fourth-down incompletion that secured the result. 

Our assessment: Six victories provide a meaningful floor, but the losing conference record limits how positively the season can be judged. The question is whether Pitt can turn a respectable overall record into a finish that demonstrates sustained progress.

The Florida State game was a missed opportunity against a team operating under an interim coach. Still, that result alone is insufficient evidence of an approaching coaching change.

Narduzzi belongs in the middle tier: accountable for uneven performance, but without the combination of severe current results and unresolved institutional patience associated with the hottest seats.

A productive finish would move the discussion toward improving the team's ceiling. Further disappointing results would keep attention on why conference consistency remains elusive.

9. Fran Brown, Syracuse

Assessment: Cooling, with both results and leadership comments supporting that judgment.

Syracuse's comeback victory at NC State was valuable beyond its effect on the standings. The Orange scored 21 fourth-quarter points to win 34-31, reaching 5-5 and preserving a route to bowl eligibility. 

Leadership support also deserves considerable weight. https://t.co/bS1z5ji41a reporter Chris Carlson reported November 13 that athletic director Bryan Blair expected Brown to lead the program in 2027. Earlier, Blair publicly described Brown as "my guy." 

My assessment: Those developments justify a clear drop from sixth to ninth. Public support cannot guarantee future employment, but it is stronger evidence than speculation built solely around a disappointing record.

Brown still needs to convert the recovery into a successful finish. The standard should include avoiding another reversal after restoring momentum.

As of the cutoff, however, the case for immediate danger is weaker than it was earlier in the season. The reporting supports patience, and the latest result supports it as well.

10. Rick Stockstill, Florida State - interim

Assessment: An encouraging audition, with the permanent appointment still unresolved.

Stockstill won his first two games as interim coach, both on the road. Florida State followed a 31-24 victory at Boston College with a 16-10 win at Pitt, improving to 5-5. 

Our assessment: Those victories strengthen his case as a stabilizing leader. The Pitt result was especially useful because Florida State protected a narrow lead through repeated defensive stops.

They do not establish that the university intends to make the appointment permanent. An interim can perform well while the institution continues pursuing a broader search.

Stockstill ranks below Goebbel because his initial results have been stronger, giving him a more favorable immediate argument. Both placements remain less directly comparable with permanent coaches' rankings.

The remaining games offer Stockstill an opportunity to secure bowl eligibility and demonstrate that the improvement can continue at home. Whatever happens in the search, restoring competitiveness would represent a meaningful contribution to a difficult season.

11. James Franklin, Virginia Tech

Assessment: November disappointment, with low immediate dismissal risk.

Virginia Tech's 40-22 home loss to Stanford was a significant setback. The Hokies fell behind early after turnovers and could not recover, dropping to 6-4. 

Franklin is in his first season following Virginia Tech's November 2025 appointment. The university introduced him as an experienced program builder capable of restoring championship contention. 

Our assessment: That mandate creates expectations, but it also implies a rebuilding process extending beyond one November.

The latest performance warrants criticism of preparation and execution. It does not, on the evidence reviewed, justify treating Franklin as an imminent dismissal candidate.

His position is best understood as pressure to establish a convincing direction. A stronger finish would help prevent the Stanford defeat from becoming the defining image of his first season.

The practical question is what Virginia Tech must improve for 2027, rather than whether one disappointing home result ends the new administration.

12. Jeff Brohm, Louisville

Assessment: Secure, with the recovery supplying a persuasive response to earlier disappointment.

Louisville's 16-14 victory at North Carolina extended its winning streak to five games and completed a 6-2 ACC schedule. The Cardinals won through defense, with a late interception securing the result. 

Our assessment: The manner of the victory matters. Louisville showed it could win a tight road game after producing more comfortable victories during the recovery.

That combination offers evidence of adaptability rather than dependence on one style of game.

Brohm drops three places toward the cooler end because sustained winning has changed the season's direction. Seven victories leave room for disappointment relative to ambitious expectations, but they offer little basis for placing him alongside coaches trying to rescue losing seasons.

The remaining evaluation concerns how high Louisville can finish and whether it can carry its progress forward. Those are competitive questions associated with a stable program, rather than strong indicators of immediate employment danger.

13. Tavita Pritchard, Stanford

Assessment: Secure, with measurable first-year progress.

Stanford's victory at Virginia Tech ended a 15-game road losing streak. Micah Ford rushed for 149 yards and three touchdowns, and the Cardinal forced three turnovers in the 40-22 win. 
Pritchard is in his first season following his November 2025 appointment. Stanford described him then as central to restoring the program's winning tradition. 

Our assessment: The Blacksburg result gives that rebuilding effort a concrete accomplishment. Breaking a prolonged road losing streak is more useful evidence than general statements about improved culture.

At 5-5, Stanford also has a meaningful opportunity to turn progress into postseason eligibility.

Pritchard's ranking reflects the combination of a new coach's reasonable runway and an encouraging latest result. Further inconsistency would identify work still required, but the evidence through November 15 favors continued investment in his development of the program.

14. Rhett Lashlee, SMU

Assessment: Secure despite a performance that demands a forceful response.

SMU's 49-7 home loss to Wake Forest was severe. The Mustangs trailed 42-0 at halftime and finished with 275 total yards, compared with Wake Forest's 535.

Our assessment: Lashlee should face direct questions about why his team was so thoroughly outplayed. A secure coach remains accountable for a performance of that magnitude.

The wider season, however, matters. SMU stood 7-3 overall with a winning conference record, a substantially different position from the teams at the top of this list.

The defeat changes the assessment of the team's current ceiling more than it establishes a convincing case for replacing the coach.

The closing games should show whether the Mustangs can correct the problems exposed by Wake Forest. A credible response would reinforce that the loss was a serious setback within a successful program rather than the beginning of a broader decline.

15. Manny Diaz, Duke

Assessment: Very secure.

Duke's 36-25 loss at Miami left the Blue Devils 7-3. The game was competitive, although Miami ultimately produced 532 yards against Duke's defense.

The defeat followed emphatic victories over Boston College and NC State. Duke won those games 47-2 and 41-3, respectively, before traveling to Miami. 

Our assessment: That sequence provides substantial evidence that Diaz's team remains capable of strong performances. Losing on the road to the conference leader does little to overturn it.

Duke still has reasons to seek improvement, including its ability to limit explosive offense against stronger opponents. Those are ordinary coaching responsibilities within a program enjoying a successful season.

The immediate conversation should center on finishing well and maximizing postseason opportunities. Through November 15, the results provide little justification for treating Diaz as a serious hot-seat candidate.

16. Jake Dickert, Wake Forest

Assessment: Extremely secure.

Wake Forest's 49-7 victory at SMU was one of the conference's strongest performances of the season. The Demon Deacons reached 9-1, recorded six rushing touchdowns and forced three turnovers. The victory also gave Wake Forest consecutive nine-win seasons. 

Our assessment: Dickert has supplied the evidence institutions seek when evaluating a coach: results, visible development and performances that exceed ordinary expectations for the program.

The SMU game demonstrated strength across multiple parts of the team. Wake Forest could control the ground game, generate takeaways and build a decisive advantage away from home.

That makes his placement near the bottom straightforward. Remaining championship and postseason stakes create pressure to win, but they do not amount to meaningful job insecurity.

The relevant questions concern how far Dickert can take this team and how Wake Forest can sustain the standard it has established.

17. Mario Cristobal, Miami

Assessment: The coolest seat in the ACC.

Miami responded to its first defeat by beating Duke 36-25, moving to 9-1 overall and remaining unbeaten in conference play. Darian Mensah threw for 382 yards as the Hurricanes regained momentum.

"Really proud of our players, our coaching staff," Cristobal said afterward. 

Our assessment: Miami's position atop the conference standings gives Cristobal the strongest combination of current results and championship opportunity in this ranking.

Expectations remain high, and the final weeks can still determine whether the season fulfills its promise. But those competitive stakes should be distinguished from uncertainty about whether the coach deserves to continue leading the program.

Cristobal's team has demonstrated an ability to respond after disappointment and remain on course in league play. As of November 15, his employment position is the most secure on this list.

The departed coaches and the decisions still ahead

Doeren and Norvell belong in the record of this season's coaching changes. They no longer belong among active coaches facing a future dismissal decision.

NC State's October 24 announcement appointed Goebbel for the remainder of the season and launched a national search. Florida State's November 1 change placed Stockstill in charge of a team that subsequently won twice. Those searches create a different kind of pressure from the evaluations facing established coaches. 

For the remaining permanent coaches, O'Brien has the most consequential finish, Key has earned immediate relief, and Swinney faces the sharpest renewed scrutiny following the latest weekend. Belichick's evaluation remains especially dependent on the closing results and the university's postseason review.

Brown's situation illustrates why these rankings must follow reporting as closely as scores. Leadership support and a successful comeback justify cooling his assessment. Elliott's extension similarly prevents a disappointing record from being treated as sufficient evidence of imminent danger.

The strongest indicators over the final weeks will be concrete ones: additional victories, competitive responses, explicit leadership statements and announced decisions. Those developments should determine the next edition more than the volume of speculation surrounding any particular coach.
