text:
Sjoe! 👻 4 323 Ghosts on the Government Payroll💸But Who Keeps Opening the Pay Window? ~ Billions, Bureaucracy and Phantom Employees💰 When Detection Becomes the Headline Instead of the Solution ~ R3.9 Billion Worth of Payroll Smoke💸 But Who's Checking the People Holding the Matches? 🔥
On 21 October 2026, National Treasury’s Medium Term Budget Policy Statement delivered a clean number that travelled quickly: 4 323 high-risk or suspicious payroll cases flagged across national and provincial departments after verification exercises that included cross-checks against the Home Affairs population register. 

An associated annual cost of roughly R3.9 billion was cited. Parliament’s Public Service Committee welcomed the process and called for investigations, recovery of funds, and stronger controls. Final confirmed numbers and actual recoveries remain pending for the 2027 Budget cycle (National Treasury, 2026).

That is the official story, repeated with striking uniformity across major outlets. It is also incomplete.

Detecting 4 323 suspicious names is not the same as dismantling the machinery that places non-existent or long-departed workers on the public payroll and keeps them paid. 

The central claim is testable: the South African state has repeatedly shown it can produce lists of irregular payroll cases; it has not yet shown it can close the access points, name the authorisers, or alter the incentives that make the practice a recurring, low-risk enterprise. 

Without that shift, every new announcement risks becoming another performance of seriousness rather than its substance.

1. The Official Curtain Rises

National Treasury’s announcement was precise and administratively impressive. Verification work matching employee records against the population register had identified 4 323 high-risk or suspicious cases. The R3.9 billion figure was attached to the broader problem of payroll irregularities. The Public Service Committee responded with calls for investigation, recovery, and tighter controls.

Mainstream coverage framed the moment as decisive progress. Reports spoke of a crackdown, of billions lost, and of institutional seriousness on display. The polished surface—large number, technological check, parliamentary applause—invited the conclusion that something fundamental had shifted.

Yet the surface remains only surface. A verification platform can identify mismatches. It cannot, by itself, explain how those mismatches were created, protected, or allowed to persist across successive budget cycles. 

The official language celebrates detection while the deeper organisational conditions that generate the detections receive secondary attention.

Sjoe!
A system that can produce a list of 4 323 suspicious names with impressive speed is also a system that somehow managed to keep those names paid until the list was produced. The competence is real. So is the timing.

Questions Stirring:
If the verification capacity exists, why does the same category of irregularity reappear with such regularity? 
What concrete meaning attaches to “stronger controls” when the officials who previously held authorising power remain in place? 
Why does public discussion still centre on the size of the latest list rather than the identity of those who signed the appointments that created it?

What these questions together reveal:
They expose the difference between diagnostic capacity and corrective capacity. A state that can detect but cannot, or will not, interrupt the production process is measuring success by the volume of its own findings rather than by the decline of the conditions that make findings necessary. 

The questions matter because they test whether citizens are being offered evidence of control or evidence of the continued need for control.

2. The Factory Floor Remains Closed to View

Ghost workers do not materialise spontaneously. They require deliberate action by people who hold system access—human-resources officers, payroll administrators, or managers with authorising authority—who insert, retain, or fail to remove records of non-existent, departed, or duplicated employees. 

Organised internal networks, rather than isolated clerical errors, provide the more plausible explanation for the scale involved.

The dominant public narrative has given this production process only glancing treatment. Coverage has celebrated the discovery of the finished product while the conditions that manufacture the product receive fragmented mention. The problem is repeatedly cast as a technical data-matching challenge rather than an organisational and incentive problem.

This framing has consequences. Treating a recurring multi-billion-rand leakage as primarily a software or verification issue obscures the human decisions that keep the leakage alive. Access rights, authorisation protocols, and the low personal risk attached to irregular payments form the actual operating environment. 

Until those elements are examined with the same energy devoted to the list itself, the list remains a symptom report.

Sjoe!
It is possible to admire the elegance of a population-register cross-check while still noticing that the same system somehow failed to notice the same category of problem before the cross-check was applied. 

The elegance does not cancel the prior blindness.

Questions Stirring:
Who holds the specific access rights that allow non-existent or departed records to remain active and paid? 
What organisational culture or informal pressure makes the insertion or retention of such records a manageable career risk? 
Why has equal journalistic and parliamentary energy not moved from “how many ghosts did we find” to “how does the factory keep its doors open”?

What these questions together reveal:
They shift attention from the output of the system to its internal logic. Detection without diagnosis of production leaves production intact. The questions matter because every rand paid to a phantom is a rand unavailable for the services the public payroll is meant to deliver. 

Understanding the factory is not optional detail; it is the difference between temporary lists and lasting change.

3. The Missing Names Behind the Names

The scarcity of specific accountability is more striking still. The public record moves easily from the aggregate figure of 4 323 cases to general calls for investigation and recovery. It moves far more slowly to the names of the officials who signed appointments, who authorised continued payments, or who ultimately received the funds. 

Final confirmed numbers and successful recoveries remain pending for the 2027 Budget.

Detection is administratively straightforward and politically useful. Naming the people who enabled the leakage is harder, more personal, and therefore rarer. The result is a public conversation comfortable with diffuse responsibility.

This is the pivotal shift. The story ceases to be about a successful verification exercise and becomes about the administrative culture that allows irregular payments to continue without personal consequence. When accountability remains collective, it remains optional.

Sjoe!
There is a particular kind of institutional relief that accompanies the production of a large, anonymous number. The number is concrete. The people behind it are not. The number can be announced. The people require decisions.

Questions Stirring:
When will the first wave of named authorisers and beneficiaries appear in the public record with clear consequence? 
What formal or informal protections currently make such naming difficult? 
If recovery of funds is a stated goal, why does the conversation still lack public timelines and individual accountability measures?

What these questions together reveal:
They test whether the commitment to recovery is matched by a commitment to visibility. Diffuse responsibility protects the system that produced the irregularity. Named responsibility changes the risk calculation for the next official who holds the same access. 

The questions matter because incentive structures respond to personal consequence far more reliably than to collective undertakings.

4. Perspective, Precedent, and the Limits of Process

Place the R3.9 billion estimate against the total public-sector wage bill of approximately R717 billion and the absolute figure remains large while the relative percentage is modest. More revealing is the historical pattern. Earlier verification exercises produced comparable findings and comparable announcements. The persistence of the problem suggests that previous clean-ups largely generated lists rather than lasting changes in behaviour or control environments.

Specialist commentary has occasionally noted links to weak internal controls and the pressures that accompany cadre deployment. Mainstream treatment has kept these observations peripheral. The current exercise is therefore not a sudden institutional awakening. It is another iteration in a long series of detection announcements.

The reader is left to judge whether process announcements constitute progress or simply the latest chapter in a recurring cycle of discovery without structural correction. A verification platform can be improved. An incentive environment that continues to reward or protect irregular authorisation requires a different order of change.

Sjoe!
There is a quiet institutional comfort in the phrase “stronger controls.” It sounds decisive. It postpones the harder question of whose behaviour, exactly, is expected to change, and under what personal cost for failing to change it.

Questions Stirring:
What measurable changes in access rights, authorisation protocols, or consequence management followed the previous verification rounds? 
If the same structural conditions remain, what independent reason exists to expect a different long-term outcome? 
How should citizens weigh a new list of suspicious cases against the continued absence of evidence that the underlying incentives have been altered?

What these questions together reveal:
They distinguish between activity and result. Process can be announced indefinitely. Result requires evidence that the conditions producing the problem have been modified. The questions matter because public finance is not an abstract ledger; it is the material basis for the services citizens are told the state exists to provide. 

Recurring leakage without recurring consequence is not a technical shortcoming. It is a governance pattern.

5. The Echo Chamber and the Unasked Question

Coverage across major outlets—IOL, Business Day, Moneyweb, TimesLIVE, News24, and SABC—displayed strong source homogeneity. Reports drew almost exclusively on the Treasury MTBPS text and parliamentary statements, recycling near-identical numbers and language. 

The flagged figure was amplified as evidence of progress. The systemic creation mechanisms, the accountability vacuum, and the incentive structures received far less sustained attention.

When the story that reaches the public is shaped so tightly by the institutions under examination, the space for probing deeper drivers shrinks. This is not a claim of conspiracy. It is a record of the narrowness of the frame.

Real accountability would look like closed access points, named authorisers facing consequence, recovered funds with clear trails, and a measurable subsequent decline in the conditions that allow irregular records to be created. 

Process announcements and new lists, however carefully prepared, do not yet meet that standard.

Sjoe!
There is a particular efficiency in a story that begins and ends with the same official paragraph. It travels well. It requires little additional reporting. It also leaves the most interesting questions outside the frame.

Questions Stirring:
Why does the public conversation remain so tightly bound to the official framing? 
What would independent scrutiny of the creation process and the incentive structure look like in practice? 
If detection is repeatedly achieved and celebrated while the underlying conditions persist, at what point does the celebration itself become part of the institutional pattern?

What these questions together reveal:
They ask whether the information environment is capable of examining the system that produces the information. A narrow frame protects the status quo more effectively than open denial. 

The questions matter because democratic accountability depends on the public’s ability to see not only the symptoms the state is willing to announce, but the structures the state is slower to examine.

Synthesis

The facts form a coherent pattern. 
National Treasury has demonstrated, once again, that it can identify large numbers of suspicious payroll cases through verification and population-register cross-checks (National Treasury, 2026). 
Parliament has called for investigation and recovery. 
The associated annual cost has been placed in the region of R3.9 billion against a wage bill of roughly R717 billion. 
Earlier verification rounds produced comparable findings without permanently altering the underlying conditions. 
Mainstream coverage has amplified the detection numbers while giving limited sustained attention to creation mechanisms, named accountability, or incentive structures.

Taken together, the independent observations support a single claim: the state is proficient at producing lists of irregular payroll cases and far less proficient at dismantling the organisational, access, and incentive conditions that generate them. 

The claim is falsifiable. It would be weakened by the appearance of named authorisers facing clear consequence, by measurable recovery of funds with transparent trails, by documented closure of the access points that allow irregular records to persist, and by a subsequent decline in the incidence of the same category of irregularity.

Until those indicators appear, the pattern remains one of detection without structural correction. 

The stakes are concrete. Every rand paid to a non-existent or long-departed worker is a rand unavailable for the services the public payroll is meant to support. The quiet persistence of the conditions that produce those payments is therefore not a technical footnote. It is a continuing test of institutional seriousness.

Objections

One objection is that detection itself constitutes progress and that the current exercise represents a meaningful step. Detection is necessary. It is not sufficient. Previous rounds of detection did not prevent the reappearance of the same problem at scale. Progress must ultimately be measured by the reduction of the conditions that make detection necessary.

A second objection is that naming individual authorisers is complex, legally constrained, and risks unfairness. Complexity is real. The absence of visible movement toward named accountability after successive detection exercises is also real. Legal process and fairness are compatible with transparency about who held the relevant access and authorisation powers.

A third objection is that the R3.9 billion figure is modest relative to the total wage bill and should not be overstated. Absolute scale matters. A recurring leakage measured in billions remains a serious failure of control regardless of its percentage of the larger bill. The relative figure does not erase the absolute one.

Conclusion

The 4 323 flagged cases and the R3.9 billion estimate are real. The verification work is real. The parliamentary calls for investigation are real. Yet the deeper pattern is also real: detection is repeatedly achieved and publicly framed as progress, while the collusion, system access, authorising officials, and incentive structures that produce the ghosts remain largely unexamined and unreformed.

Citizens are entitled to more than lists. They are entitled to evidence that the access points have been closed, that the people who kept irregular records active have faced consequence, and that the next verification round will find a smaller problem because the conditions that created the previous one have been changed. 

Until that evidence appears, every new announcement of suspicious cases risks remaining what the pattern so far suggests it is: another carefully prepared statement about a problem the system still does not appear ready to stop.

The converging evidence shows that detecting ghost workers is not the same as dismantling the system that creates them.

text:
Good morning, humans     o.🍎I🍎.o

What do you know about apples ?

      Two stories to embark the musical explanation of the fruit and their interpretations in different cultures... and there is way more then this:

1. The origin of truth...          and      2.   After Life...

1. The origin of truth...

Apple origin : 

     The rugged mountain slopes of the Tian Shan range in Kazakhstan.
Wild Ancestor: The wild species Malus sieversii is the direct ancestor of the modern cultivated apple.
Spread: Ancient traders and animals carried the seeds along the Silk Road.
Genetics: Modern DNA studies prove that most cultivated apples trace their roots back to these Kazakh forests.
Wild Ancestor: The tough and sweet Malus sieversii is the primary genetic parent of nearly all modern apples.
Almaty's Name: The largest city in Kazakhstan, Almaty, translates to "father of apples" or "full of apples".
Early Spread: Bears and birds first carried the seeds, and human traders along the Silk Road later spread them toward Europe and Asia.

    The apple of discord (lesser known myths,Greek mythology)

    The apple of discord is a Greek mythology tale where Eris, the goddess of chaos, tossed a golden apple inscribed "To the fairest" into a royal wedding. It sparked a fierce quarrel among three goddesses Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite that led directly to the Trojan War.

The Wedding and the Golden Apple The Snub: 
     The sea goddess Thetis and her husband Peleus held a grand wedding. They did not invite Eris, the goddess of strife, because she only brought fights and bad moods.The Revenge: Mad about the slight, Eris crashed the party anyway. She threw a bright golden apple onto the banquet table.The Inscription: Words were carved into the apple that said "Kalliste" or "To the fairest"

The Fight of the Goddesses The Claims:
     Three powerful goddesses immediately wanted the apple: Hera (queen of the gods), Athena (goddess of wisdom), and Aphrodite (goddess of love).The Deadlock: No other god dared to say who was the best or most beautiful, as picking one meant making the other two enemies for life.The Choice: Zeus refused to pick, so he sent them to a young shepherd and prince of Troy named Paris.

The Judgment of Paris The Bribes: 

    The goddesses tried to buy his vote. Hera promised him supreme power and control over Asia. Athena promised him glory and skill in every battle. Aphrodite made the best offer: she promised him Helen, the most beautiful mortal woman alive.The Winner: Paris gave the golden apple to Aphrodite.

The Result The Abduction: Paris sailed to Sparta and won Helen away from her husband, King Menelaus. Some versions say she fell in love with him, while others say Aphrodite used magic.
     The War: When Paris took Helen back to Troy, the angry Greek kings joined forces under Agamemnon and sailed to attack Troy, starting a ten year war....

More known religious concepts about the apple:

    In the Book of Genesis, the forbidden fruit in the Garden of Eden is only called peri, a generic Hebrew word for "fruit". The popular idea that Eve ate an apple comes from a Latin wordplay in the 4th century and old European art.

The Real Biblical StoryThe Rule: 

      God told Adam and Eve they could eat from any tree in the garden except one. That was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.The Test: A talking serpent tempted Eve. It told her she would not die, but would become like God.The Choice: Eve saw that the fruit looked good and wanted wisdom. She picked it, ate it, and gave some to Adam, who was with her.The Result: Their eyes opened to their nakedness, they felt shame, and God sent them out of the garden.

How the Apple Became Famous The Latin Pun: 

       When St. Jerome translated the Bible into Latin, he used the word malum. In Latin, malum means both "evil" and an apple-like fruit.The Art: Medieval and Renaissance painters in Europe used the familiar local apple as a symbol for sin and the forbidden fruit in their artwork...  

        Summarising: What is the concept of the apple in history religion and conceptual meaning.

    The apple is a rich symbol across human history, representing temptation and original sin in Christianity, immortality and wisdom in Greek mythology, and health or discord in secular culture, bridging ideas of desire, knowledge, and mortality for thousands of years.

    Religion and Myth Forbidden Fruit: 
    Abrahamic traditions link the apple to the tree of knowledge of good and evil in Eden, though the Bible just says "fruit."Greek Mythology: Oranges and apples mixed in tales; the Golden Apple of Discord sparked the Trojan War, and the Garden of the Hesperides held immortal apples.Norse Tradition: Goddess Idun kept golden apples that gave the Norse gods eternal youth.

History and Science Origins: 

     Wild apples started in the mountains of Central Asia.The Silk Road: Travelers carried seeds across Asia and Europe.Newton's Apple: A falling apple helped Isaac Newton think about gravity.

Conceptual Meaning Knowledge, Symbolism: 

It stands for learning, truth, and forbidden wisdom.Temptation: It represents human desire and choice. Health: The old saying links eating one to good wellness.
Desire and Refreshment:
     In poetic books, the apple represents physical delight, fragrance, and comfort.
    The Myth of Temptation: Culturally, the conceptual idea of the "apple" shifted to symbolize human disobedience, the loss of innocence, and the transition from a state of pure trust to moral accountability.
      In Western art, the apple stands for the sin of Adam and Eve. Love and Beauty: Ancient Greek art links the apple to Aphrodite, the goddess of love. Life and Death: Decaying apples or apple cores represent the passing of time and human mortality (vanitas).

2. After Life... 

      The connection between apples and life after death is deeply rooted in ancient mythology, where the fruit acts as a bridge, a key and a source of rebirth across the veil of mortality. Across many cultures, apples represent the food of the gods that grants immortality, meaning that to hold or eat an apple after death is to live forever. 

Here is how the apple connects the physical world to the afterlife: 

The Celtic Realm of Avalon (The Isle of Apples): 
In Celtic mythology, the ultimate resting place for heroes and souls is Avalon, which literally translates to "The Isle of Apples." 
The Bridge to Afterlife:
 It was a mythical island paradise where apple trees were always in bloom and bore fruit year-round. 
Burial Ritual: 
The Celts frequently buried apples in graves alongside the deceased. The fruit served as a magical passport and sustained the soul, allowing lovers and families to find each other in the Next World and achieve spiritual rebirth.

 Norse Mythology:
 Iðunn’s Apples of Youth: In Norse myth, the gods are not naturally immortal; they require a specific source of life to keep them from aging and dying.
Defeating Death: 
The goddess Iðunn (Idun) guards a casket of magical golden apples.
Eternal Renewal: 
When the gods begin to grow old and approach the shadow of death, they eat these apples to instantly restore their youth, effectively conquering death and maintaining their eternal existence.

 Greek Mythology: 
The Golden Apples of the Hesperides: For the ancient Greeks, the Golden Apples grew in a sacred orchard at the westernmost edge of the world, closely tied to the sunset (which symbolized the end of life).The Reward of Immortality: These apples grew on a tree given to Hera by Gaia. They granted immortality and divine status to anyone who ate them.

The Elysian Connection: 
The garden was located near the Elysian Fields, the Greek afterlife for the virtuous. The apple represented the ultimate prize of an eternal life free from the decay of the underworld. 

The Symbolism: If you are connecting the apple to a couple staying together after death, the apple represents the food of eternity. While their physical bodies might perish, sharing or holding the apple ensures their souls bypass the standard decay of death, allowing them to step into an everlasting paradise together. 

In mythology, the apple is the ultimate symbol of eternal love, fertility, and the bridge between life and death. While apples themselves grant immortality to the gods in various traditions, the specific myth about a devoted couple whose love keeps them together as intertwined trees even after death is actually the Greek myth of Philemon and Baucis.

Though they are turned into an oak and a linden tree (rather than an apple tree), their story is deeply intertwined with the broader ancient tradition of using sacred trees and fruits—especially apples—to represent a love that survives the grave.

The Ultimate Myth of love after life:
     Philemon and Baucis: In this famous story from Ovid's Metamorphoses, an impoverished, elderly couple named Philemon and Baucis unknowingly welcome the gods Zeus and Hermes into their home after all their wealthy neighbors turn them away. The Reward: Touched by the couple’s deep hospitality and lifelong devotion to each other, Zeus offers to grant them any wish. The Wish: They ask that they may serve the gods together and, most importantly, that neither would ever have to live a day without the other or see the other's grave. The Afterlife Union: When they finally reach the end of their exceptionally long lives, the gods transform them simultaneously. Philemon turns into a mighty oak tree, and Baucis into a gentle linden tree, their branches forever intertwined, allowing them to stay together for eternity.

The Apple as the Symbol of Marriage and Eternal Union: 

    While Philemon and Baucis became the oak and linden, the apple tree and its fruit carry the specific mythological weight of binding couples together in life and the afterlife:

Greek Wedding Seals:
     In ancient Greece, the primordial goddess Gaia gave an apple tree to Hera on her wedding day to Zeus, to symbolize an eternal, unbreakable union. From then on, newlywed couples in Athens would share and eat an apple before entering the bridal chamber, to ensure lasting love and fertility.

The Proposal: Tossing an apple at someone was the ancient Greek equivalent of a marriage proposal. Catching it meant the recipient accepted your love and committed their life to yours. The Celtic Avalon (The Isle of Apples): In Celtic mythology, the apple is the exact bridge between love and the afterlife. The mythical paradise Avalon literally translates to the 'Isle of Apples.' It is a realm of eternal youth, where souls go after death. The Celts frequently buried apples in the graves of lovers, so they would have the food of rebirth to find each other and stay sustained in the Next World.

text:
layerzero:native — THE CROSS-CHAIN VALUE CAPTURE BET
⠀
A roughly $604 MILLION cryptocurrency.
⠀
Approximately 400 MILLION tokens circulating.
⠀
Infrastructure connecting applications across independent blockchains.
⠀
And a token trading approximately 80% below its all-time high.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
LayerZero helps assets and messages move between chains.
⠀
Yet the fees paid to operate that infrastructure do not automatically flow to ZRO holders.
⠀
Stargate-funded buybacks are active.
⠀
The LayerZero protocol fee switch remains inactive.
⠀
Is layerzero:native an overlooked bet on cross-chain finance?
⠀
Or is adoption growing faster than the token's ability to capture value?
⠀
Let's examine the numbers.
⠀
01 | WHAT IS LAYERZERO?
⠀
LayerZero is a cross-chain messaging protocol.
⠀
It allows applications on different blockchains to communicate.
⠀
Bridges, token transfers, and other cross-chain applications can use that messaging infrastructure.
⠀
Its architecture separates:
⠀
• Endpoints that handle messages
• Decentralized Verifier Networks that verify them
• Executors that deliver verified messages
⠀
Applications configure their verification requirements.
⠀
The investment thesis is that a multichain financial system needs reliable communication infrastructure.
⠀
The token thesis requires an additional step:
⠀
That infrastructure must generate sustainable demand for ZRO.
⠀
02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER
⠀
November 17, 2026 snapshot:
⠀
ZRO Price: ~$1.51
Market Cap: ~$604M
FDV: ~$1.51B
Circulating Supply: ~399.98M ZRO
Total Supply: 1B ZRO
Maximum Supply: 1B ZRO
Circulating / Total Supply: ~40%
24H Trading Volume: ~$78.1M
All-Time High: ~$7.47
Decline From ATH: ~79.8%
⠀
MESSAGING ECONOMICS:
⠀
DefiLlama 30D Fees: ~$421,755
DefiLlama 30D Protocol Revenue: $0 reported
⠀
These figures describe the tracked messaging business.
⠀
They should not be treated as a consolidated income statement covering Stargate and LayerZero Labs.
⠀
03 | THE CROSS-CHAIN OPPORTUNITY
⠀
Stablecoins, tokenized assets, and applications increasingly operate across multiple networks.
⠀
That creates demand for moving information and value between them.
⠀
Potential customers include:
⠀
• Stablecoin issuers
• Tokenized asset platforms
• Wallets
• Exchanges
• DeFi applications
• Institutional settlement systems
⠀
LayerZero's opportunity is to become infrastructure embedded inside those products.
⠀
But the dollar value transferred is not revenue.
⠀
A billion dollars moving across chains does not mean a billion dollars of economic value accrues to ZRO.
⠀
04 | THE FEE CONTRADICTION
⠀
Cross-chain messages require verification and execution.
⠀
Users pay for those services.
⠀
DVNs and Executors receive compensation for performing them.
⠀
Those payments are economically different from a protocol fee used to purchase ZRO.
⠀
That distinction explains why a messaging protocol can report substantial activity while reporting no protocol revenue under a particular methodology.
⠀
Investors need to follow the payment destination.
⠀
Activity measures usage.
⠀
Retained revenue and token purchases reveal value capture.
⠀
05 | THE BUYBACK MODEL
⠀
ZRO already has an operating buyback mechanism through Stargate.
⠀
Stargate generates revenue from cross-chain products.
⠀
LayerZero states that, starting in April 2026, 100% of Stargate revenue goes toward ZRO purchases.
⠀
The Foundation's tracker currently reports:
⠀
Total ZRO Purchased: ~2.72M
Cumulative Cost Basis: ~$3.98M
Share of Total Supply: ~0.27%
⠀
October 2026 purchases:
⠀
~183,875 ZRO for ~$299,716.
⠀
These are observable purchases rather than a purely hypothetical future mechanism.
⠀
But their scale still matters.
⠀
Buying tokens does not automatically mean those tokens are permanently burned.
⠀
06 | THE PROTOCOL FEE SWITCH
⠀
The official buyback tracker lists the LayerZero protocol fee switch as inactive.
⠀
This is separate from Stargate's active purchases.
⠀
LayerZero also introduced commercial pricing changes effective September 1:
⠀
• Stargate OFT transfer fees of up to 2 basis points, capped at $250
• A $0.25 minimum LayerZero Labs Executor fee
⠀
The Stargate transfer fee applies to transfers through its app.
⠀
Other interfaces and direct integrations are not automatically subject to that product fee.
⠀
These changes do not activate the protocol fee switch.
⠀
Higher pricing could improve monetization.
⠀
It could also encourage customers to compare alternative routes and providers.
⠀
07 | THE SUPPLY QUESTION
⠀
ZRO has a maximum supply of 1 billion tokens.
⠀
Approximately 40% is currently classified as circulating.
⠀
That leaves a substantial difference between circulating market capitalization and fully diluted valuation.
⠀
A fixed maximum supply does not eliminate dilution risk for current holders.
⠀
Existing locked tokens can still enter circulation.
⠀
Investors should distinguish:
⠀
• Maximum supply
• Unlocked supply
• Circulating supply
• Tokens actually offered for sale
⠀
These are different measurements.
⠀
Neither an unlock nor a treasury transfer automatically becomes an exchange sale.
⠀
08 | THE NEXT UNLOCK
⠀
DefiLlama lists the next unlock for November 19, 2026.
⠀
Estimated amount:
⠀
23.63 MILLION ZRO.
⠀
Approximately 5.91% of the reported circulating supply.
⠀
At roughly $1.51, that represents about $35.7 million.
⠀
The tracked allocations include core contributors and strategic partners.
⠀
For perspective, that token amount is roughly 129 times October's Stargate-funded purchases.
⠀
This compares two different flows:
⠀
An unlock increases transferability.
⠀
A buyback creates an actual purchase.
⠀
It does not mean all unlocked tokens will be sold.
⠀
But it shows why current buybacks cannot simply be assumed to neutralize potential supply pressure.
⠀
09 | THE SECURITY AND COMPETITIVE TEST
⠀
LayerZero lets applications configure their security.
⠀
That flexibility is useful.
⠀
It also makes verification choices, confirmation settings, and application administration important.
⠀
Investors should examine the security configuration behind each major integration.
⠀
A broad ecosystem label is not a substitute for understanding its trust assumptions.
⠀
The commercial test is equally demanding:
⠀
Can LayerZero retain customers while charging enough to support meaningful token purchases?
⠀
Integration depth can strengthen customer retention.
⠀
It does not guarantee unlimited pricing power.
⠀
10 | THE ZERO EXPANSION
⠀
The thesis now extends beyond messaging.
⠀
LayerZero is developing Zero, a Layer 1 intended for financial and institutional workloads.
⠀
Its stated plans connect future network economics to ZRO.
⠀

His Excellency Mikheil Kavelashvili

Subject: Building Diplomatic Relations and Strategic Partnerships with the Republic of Balochistan: An Invitation to International Recognition and Cooperation

Excellencies,
Georgia declared independence in 1918, lost it to Soviet annexation in 1921, and restored it in 1991. Georgians have since faced conflicts affecting their territorial integrity and have pursued democratic reform and closer integration with Europe.
We admire Georgia's resilience and its ancient culture and traditions. Balochistan offers its goodwill and hopes for friendship.

The history of Balochistan
Balochistan is not a newcomer to sovereignty. The Khanate of Kalat held a distinct treaty relationship with the British Crown (1876) and was never part of British India’s princely states. On 4 August 1947, at a round-table meeting in Delhi attended by Lord Mountbatten, Mohammad Ali Jinnah and the Khan of Kalat, Mir Ahmad Yar Khan, it was agreed that Kalat (Balochistan) would become an independent sovereign state with a status different from that of the Indian princely states.
On 11 August 1947, three days before Pakistan came into being, Balochistan declared its independence from British rule. The announcement was published in the New York Times and broadcast by All India Radio on 12 August 1947. A standstill agreement with the new Dominion of Pakistan followed.

Kalat’s bicameral parliament, the Dar-ul-Awam (House of commons) and the Dar-ul-Umara (House of lords), unanimously rejected accession to Pakistan when it met in December 1947 and February 1948. On 27 March 1948 Pakistan illegally invaded and annexed Balochistan. The Baloch have never regarded this as a free act: the Khan and Jinnah were photographed together on other occasions, yet not a single photograph of the signing of the accession instrument has been published, which is consistent with our position that it was never a mutual agreement.

Since 1948 the Baloch people have continued to assert their right to independence and sovereignty, through political action, diplomatic manners and, at times, defensive armed resistance (1948, 1958, 1962, 1973–77 and since the early 2000s). Millions of Baloch, scattered across the globe but united in purpose, are raising one voice under the leadership of Hyrbyair Marri, President of the Free Balochistan Movement. They call on the nations of the world to recognize the Republic of Balochistan as an independent state, a recognition it has earned and rightfully deserves.
The Baloch nation has long suffered the plunder of its resources, enforced disappearances, ethnic cleansing, and relentless repression by Pakistan. Across the western part of Balochistan, the Baloch people face the same fate under Iranian rule: fabricated encounters, mass executions, expulsion from their own land, and the denial of birth certificates and legal identity, a deliberate effort to erase their existence.

The significance of Balochistan
Balochistan sits where South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East meet, on the Arabian Sea coast just outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil passes. It is a natural gateway for global trade. Two globally important deep-sea ports lie on the Baloch coast: Chabahar, which is under Iran’s illegal rule, and Gwadar, which is under Pakistan’s unlawful rule. Beneath the land lie Balochistan’s mineral resources include copper, gold, chromite, coal, natural gas, lead, zinc, barite, iron ore, limestone, gypsum, marble, granite, onyx, magnesite, sulphur, fluorite, antimony, manganese, bauxite, celestite, rock salt, silica sand, fuller’s earth, lapis lazuli, agate, and reported traces of uranium and rare earth elements of strategic value, including the Reko Diq and Saindak deposits and the Sui gas field.

Because the Republic of Balochistan declared independence on 11 August 1947, we, the Baloch, consider ourselves independent. A free, Secular, democratic and stable Balochistan is vital for regional and global peace and for connectivity between the Indian Ocean and the heartland of Eurasia.

Balochistan offers: Building Partnerships for Peace, Security, and Sustainable Development

Georgia is a Black Sea and Caucasus transit hub with a proud and ancient national identity. It sits at a crossroads that links Europe and Asia. The country is committed to protecting its sovereignty and its trade corridors. It is navigating political divisions and regional security pressures with resolve. A free, stable Balochistan, at the meeting-point of Eurasia and the Indian Ocean, can be a natural partner in this journey. It can contribute to peace, security and connectivity across the region.

The Republic of Balochistan offers your country:
• Black Sea–Indian Ocean link: Georgia’s ports and rail as a connecting node for Eurasian trade.
• Connectivity: rail, road and pipeline links between the Indian Ocean and Central Asia, with your country as a partner and a beneficiary.
• Trade and ports: access to Balochistan’s Arabian Sea ports and transit corridors, giving your exporters and importers a new gateway to South Asia, Central Asia and the Gulf.
• Energy: long-term, preferential supply agreements for natural gas and other energy resources from Balochistan, and joint development of its large solar and wind potential.

Our request
On behalf of the Republic of Balochistan, we respectfully ask your Government to:
1. Recognize the Republic of Balochistan as an independent state and establish diplomatic relations;
2. Support appropriate observer-level engagement for Balochistan at the United Nations and, in line with each Organization’s own procedures, at the European Union, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and the African Union.
3. Stand with the Baloch in nation-building: education, health, infrastructure, technology, defense and security.

The commitments in this letter are those of the Republic of Balochistan as it takes up the effective exercise of sovereignty over its territory and resources; we make them in good faith so that your Government can plan with us from the outset.

Partnership with Balochistan is of real benefit to your country and to the world. We would welcome the opportunity to meet your representatives at the earliest convenience.

With our highest consideration,
THE REPUBLIC OF BALOCHISTAN

Mir Yar Baloch
Representative for the Republic of Balochistan

Laura Ingraham: From how we finally resolved the Iran situation to his possible 2028 run, we covered a lot of ground with Vice President Vance. The president on his way to Asia, this is going to be probably another historic meeting. Sure. The Democrats, you can kind of see what's already in the works. They're going to be arguing, given the Nvidia situation, Jensen Huang's closeness to President Trump, that he's actually too soft on China. That these tech CEOs aren't so much American companies, they're more global companies, always pushing the envelope on dealing with China, opening up markets to China. What is your view on that, given the fact that you're known to be more of a China hawk? Sure. Obviously this program is as well. But what is a potential pitfall for the United States, both politically and national security wise?

JD Vance: So the Democrats have said a lot of absurd things the last couple of years, but them pretending to be China hawks, Laura, I don't think that any of the American people actually buy this. The way to be tough on China is not to saber rattle and start a war with the country, it's to reindustrialize the United States of America. And what the president, his approach to being tough on China is, yes, have good diplomatic relations, have smart diplomacy with the PRC, but the way to make ourselves strong against Chinese influence is to build more of our own stuff, is to make more of our own stuff. Chinese leverage over the United States of America, it doesn't come because they're better at saber rattling than the United States of America. It comes because 40 years of bipartisan leadership allowed the PRC to control our industrial supply chain. When another country controls your food, your medicine, your technology industry, that is how they control the United States of America. What Donald Trump's tough on China policy has been is make Americans control more of our own stuff. That has been wildly successful, and it's one of the reasons why he has a good relationship with President Xi, because President Xi respects him. He sees him as somebody who's actually tough and smart, rather than somebody that you can take advantage of, like so many other American presidents.

Laura Ingraham: What do we know about this Alice Huang woman? Because there seems to be a lot of confusion as to whether she was a Chinese spy, or she wasn't a Chinese spy, we heard that Marco Rubio had told the president that we believe she's a Chinese asset. The president today said it's not clear that she is, and meanwhile the Wall Street Journal said Jensen Huang is basically given a back door to China for its own advanced chip development, given the fact that we have allowed Malaysia to develop these data centers, leakage through to China and all that. But the question is, is she a spy or isn't she? Why can't we get an answer to that question?

JD Vance: Well, the reason is because this intelligence always points in different directions, right? The thing I've learned about intelligence, Laura, I think Henry Kissinger once said that you think you're really smart by reading all the intelligence, and then you realize that because the intelligence disagrees with itself, and I think what the president is just pointing at is, there is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know, and he doesn't know, whether this woman was a spy or not, but that actually is not the main issue. The main issue is we need to reindustrialize the country and protect our critical technology and our critical infrastructure, and the only way to do that is to build more of it in the United States of America and prevent it from falling into the wrong hands. Now, again, I find it just hysterical that the Democrats are accusing Donald Trump of being soft on China when it comes to export controls, when it comes to ensuring that American chips, the most advanced American chips, stay with American technology providers. Nobody has been better on this than the Trump administration, so I really think that what the Democrats are doing is they're using a lot of innuendo, and they're using this very salacious story about Jensen Huang and this mistress, and they're trying to effectively accuse Donald Trump of doing what Joe Biden did for four years.

Laura Ingraham: So you're not concerned that a third-party country has been able to get that technology from Nvidia and then back door to China?

JD Vance: Well, certainly I'm concerned about it, Laura. It's our job to be concerned about this stuff. So we have these export controls, and then there are all kinds of companies that are set up to try to end-run around those export controls to try to hide from the fact that they're actually working with the PRC. So that's just something we have to stay on top of, but I think our administration has been more on top of it than any administration in American history.

Laura Ingraham: You made a lot of news with your post midterm posting on X about really the cause of the massive loss for Republicans, losing Mississippi, losing Texas. It was just across the board, wipeout, as you called it, a shellacking. You said the Iran war was really the major reason for the Republicans losing. Is there daylight between you and the president on this issue today that the American people should know about or that informs your current thinking?

JD Vance: No, there's no daylight, Laura. The President of the United States, he makes decisions, and obviously within the administration we have debates and discussions about exactly what to do. When the president makes a decision, he is owed a cabinet that helps implement that decision, and I think there's no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration. Now politically, yes, and I think the president himself has absolutely said this as well. There was a political cost, the higher gas prices, the higher energy prices, and the thing that I try to remind people is that higher energy prices are the consequence not just of what's going on in the Middle East, but of the fact that we've under-invested in American energy infrastructure for decades. Why haven't we built a refinery since the 1970s? That increases energy costs. Why do we spend trillions of dollars on a green new scam rather than actually building out our own oil and gas facilities?

Laura Ingraham: But they're blaming you for this memorandum of understanding that that was somehow the reason Republicans didn't win in Iran, and to that I thought, well, wait a second. There was this magic plan out there about how to get Iran to cave, and the president decided, oh, I'm not going to do that?

JD Vance: No, it's people who want to criticize the president of the United States but frankly don't have the courage to criticize the president, so they criticize the vice president, and Laura, you know, that's what you sign up for. I'm happy to be a heat shield for the president of the United States, but the fundamental reality is we have accomplished an extraordinary amount. We have destroyed the nuclear program. We have destroyed Iran's conventional military, and there is this category of people who just seem to want the war to go on forever. They want to keep on going and keep on going. The president of the United States has a lot of options, right? He could say we're done now. He could, of course, exert more military and diplomatic pressure on the Iranians. I think it's something he's thinking about doing right now, right? What are we actually going to do to finally bring this thing to a resolution? But my prediction, Laura, is that whatever the president ultimately decides to do, there are going to be people who demand more, who want the war to go on indefinitely. And what I feel quite confident about the president of the United States, and again, there's no daylight here, is that whatever he ultimately decides to do, however he ultimately decides to bring the conflict to a close, he is not going to let this become a forever war. And the people who want it to become a forever war, they can attack me all they want to because we signed up to not do this. We told the American people we would do no more forever wars. Yes, the president felt he had to destroy the nuclear program, and yes, the Iranian nuclear program is a threat to the United States of America, but we are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or frankly, even a two-year commitment, despite the fact that a lot of neo-conservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever. We're not going to stay there forever. We promised we wouldn't, and I have full confidence the president will get us out of this thing with great results for the American people.

Laura Ingraham: I know we're almost out of time. Your friend, Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan has said that it's going to be a delicious irony that you're going to have to swear him in as the next senator from the state of Michigan. You probably have a few minutes to chat with him after that happens. What might you talk about?

JD Vance: Well, I hope we can talk about how to best serve the people of Michigan and the United States of America. I really love the working-class citizens, all of the citizens of Michigan. I think they're hardworking people. They build amazing products with great American craftsmanship, and if Abdul El-Sayed wants to work with me and the president to make those people's lives better, he's going to find us very much a willing partner. I hope Democrats actually try to govern on what they ran on, because if you look at what they ran on, what do they talk about? Reindustrializing America, lowering energy costs for Americans. They ran on a lot of the themes that Donald Trump ran on in 2024, "Let's work together." I'm not worried about the politics of this. I'm worried about getting results for the people of Michigan, the people of the country, and if Senator El-Sayed wants to help us with that, he'll find a willing partner.

Laura Ingraham: 2028. I know you don't want to talk about it. You said spring you'll make a decision.

JD Vance: Yeah, we'll figure it out sometime next year.

Laura Ingraham: Is that still a hard kind of understanding on your mind?

JD Vance: You know, I'm not an expert in this, Laura, but my understanding with a presidential campaign is there's a lot of infrastructure that you have to set up, fundraising, all that stuff, and so you can't declare a month before the Iowa caucus that you're going to run for president, so I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year.

Laura Ingraham: But when you make a decision, you're all in.

JD Vance: When I make a decision, Laura, I will be all in on whatever that decision is.

Laura Ingraham: All right. Mr. Vice President, thank you so much.

JD Vance: Thank you, Laura.

Laura Ingraham: Great to see you.

JD Vance is right on the core points from his interview with Laura Ingraham Monday night. On Iran he said people who want a forever war “can attack me all they want to because we signed up to not do this,” and that Trump “is not going to let this become a forever war.” He added they won’t allow a 10- or 15-year commitment or even a two-year one. Destroy the nuclear program, then leave. That matches what voters want.

Vance said there’s “no daylight” between him and Trump on the midterms. Higher energy prices from the war and decades of underinvestment in American energy infrastructure both contributed. He noted Democrats ran in 2026 on some of the same themes Trump used in 2024 and said Republicans now have to deliver more wins on affordability and infrastructure.

On the FAA he pointed out the system still runs on 50-year-old technology and that full modernization requires Congress to fund it rather than more patchwork fixes. He said Democrats could help rebuild it if they set aside other fights and focus on the affordability and infrastructure themes they ran on.

Vance also addressed critics who blame him for the Iran talks falling apart. He said those people “want to criticize POTUS but frankly don’t have the courage to criticize the president,” so they go after the vice president instead. He called himself happy to be a heat shield. That keeps the focus on results instead of internal score-settling.

On 2028, Vance said he hasn’t made a decision and will figure it out sometime next year. He noted a presidential campaign needs real infrastructure and fundraising, so you can’t declare a month before the Iowa caucus. He said he’ll be all-in on whatever he decides. The timing is practical. Finish the current job first.

The through-line is clear. Vance is treating the midterms as a signal to go harder on America First priorities—lower energy costs, working infrastructure, and no open-ended foreign commitments—rather than retreating to the old Republican approach. Voters want results on costs and competence. Delivering those is how the party recovers.

Me: Stoner

Ai: Stoner by John Williams is a literary novel published in 1965 that explores the quiet complexities of an ordinary man's life, examining love, ambition, disappointment, loneliness, and the search for meaning. Although initially overlooked, the novel has since become widely celebrated as a masterpiece of American literature.
The story follows William Stoner, a young man born into a poor farming family in rural Missouri at the end of the nineteenth century. Sent to the University of Missouri to study agriculture, he unexpectedly discovers a passion for literature and philosophy. This discovery transforms the direction of his life, leading him to abandon farming and pursue an academic career as an English professor.
Through Stoner's experiences, the novel traces his journey through marriage, fatherhood, professional rivalries, romantic relationships, and personal struggles. His life is marked by missed opportunities, emotional isolation, unfulfilled ambitions, and circumstances he often feels powerless to change. Yet beneath the apparent ordinariness of his existence lies a profound commitment to education, literature, and intellectual integrity.
One of the novel's central themes is the idea that a life does not need to be extraordinary to be meaningful. Williams explores the quiet dignity of perseverance, the limitations of human choice, the complexity of relationships, and the ways in which personal fulfillment can emerge from seemingly insignificant experiences.

Why read this book?
Self-discovery: Explores how discovering one's true interests can fundamentally change the direction of a life.
Purpose and meaning: Examines whether an ordinary life can still be considered a meaningful and successful one.
Human relationships: Offers a deeply realistic portrayal of marriage, love, family, friendship, and emotional distance.
Resilience: Illustrates the importance of maintaining personal convictions despite disappointment and adversity.
The value of knowledge: Celebrates literature, education, intellectual curiosity, and the lifelong pursuit of understanding.

Overall: Stoner is a deeply moving meditation on the human condition. It reminds readers that greatness is not always measured by wealth, recognition, achievement, or social status. Sometimes it is found in the quiet pursuit of what one loves, the ability to endure life's disappointments, and the courage to remain faithful to one's inner values. It is a particularly powerful book for anyone interested in understanding human nature, personal identity, and what it truly means to live a life.

EVENSTAD FOR U.S. SENATE: IF ELECTED, I WILL SUSPEND MY 2028 PRESIDENTIAL EXPLORATORY BID TO FOCUS 100% ON MINNESOTA WORKING FAMILIES
Thomas Evenstad, lifelong Edina resident, public-safety advocate, architect of the Violently Dangerous Persons Act (VDP Act / Mariah’s Law), and Republican candidate for the United States Senate seat being vacated by Amy Klobuchar, today announced that if elected Minnesota’s next U.S. Senator he will immediately suspend his exploratory 2028 bid for the White House.
“Minnesota families come first,” Evenstad said. “The special election for this open Senate seat is not a stepping stone and not a branding exercise. If the people of Minnesota send me to Washington, I will put every ounce of energy into delivering results for them. The 2028 presidential exploratory effort will be suspended so I can focus 100 percent on the job Minnesota voters hire me to do.”
Evenstad is running in the 2027 special election (Republican primary August 10, 2027; general election November 2, 2027). He is calling on grassroots Minnesotans to support the campaign now—before the usual herd of establishment RINOs and career politicians flood the field and lock out outsider candidates who put working families ahead of party machines.
Day-One Priorities for Working Families
If elected, Evenstad’s first actions will center on these five priorities:
Public Safety First — Advance the Violently Dangerous Persons Act (VDP Act / Mariah’s Law) to expand civil-commitment tools against the most violently dangerous repeat offenders and deliver the projected major reduction in violent crime that Minnesota families have been denied for decades.
Kitchen-Table Cost Relief — Fight for real reductions in the everyday costs crushing working families: groceries, rent, childcare, healthcare premiums, gas, utilities, and property taxes. Results over rhetoric.
Secure Borders and End Sanctuary Policies — Support full enforcement of immigration law, end catch-and-release, and stop the flow of fentanyl and criminal aliens that hit working neighborhoods hardest.
Protect Children — Harden soft targets such as schools and churches, remove radical gender ideology and sexualized content from K-12 classrooms, and put parents back in charge of their kids’ education and safety.
Fiscal Discipline and Accountability — Cut wasteful federal spending that drives inflation and higher taxes, demand measurable results from every dollar spent, and reject the bipartisan habit of protecting institutions instead of protecting citizens.
“These are not talking points. These are the daily realities sitting on the kitchen tables of Minnesota families,” Evenstad said. “Public safety, lower costs, secure borders, protected children, and a government that finally works for the people who pay the bills. That is the job.”
Evenstad is asking for immediate grassroots support to build an independent campaign capable of competing against well-funded establishment candidates. He emphasizes that early contributions and volunteer energy are essential before the field fills with the same political class that has repeatedly shut out outsiders.
“This seat is opening soon. The machine will try to fill it with another predictable, managed candidate. I am asking ordinary Minnesotans to step in first—before the RINOs and careerists arrive,” Evenstad said. “Help me cross the thresholds, build the infrastructure, and put working families at the center of this race. Minnesota’s last stand starts with you.”
About Thomas Evenstad
Thomas Evenstad is a lifelong Minnesota resident living in Edina. He is the Republican candidate for the 2027 special election for the U.S. Senate seat currently held by Amy Klobuchar. He is the architect of the Violently Dangerous Persons Act and campaigns as a public-safety-first Republican populist who puts results for working families above party labels.

AI running on your own computer can now operate desktop applications, rather than only answer questions. Unsloth Studio’s computer-use beta lets supported local vision models and connected providers inspect screenshots and control the mouse and keyboard on Windows, macOS and Linux. The feature is off by default, with approval before initial actions and unfamiliar apps, plus user takeover. The implementation’s short demonstration used a drawn desktop; reliable performance on ordinary workflows is not established.

Powerful AI systems could face checks before becoming available in India. NDTV Profit reports, citing people familiar with the matter, that officials are considering pre-launch safety tests for the most capable models. Its sources describe a possible consultation and later legislation, but these are reported proposals. No published draft or official confirmation of those provisions was located in the research check.

Certain organizations deploying high-risk AI must assess its potential effects on fundamental rights. The European Commission has published a draft questionnaire to guide that assessment under the AI Act, developed with input from the European Union’s rights agency. Feedback closes January fifteen, twenty twenty-seven. The existing duty applies from December two, twenty twenty-seven; the consultation concerns a draft aid, rather than a new legal obligation.

Robot AI needs to connect predictions about the physical world with actions. Huawei describes CloudRobo-WM1.2 as combining a model that predicts what happens next with an architecture that generates robot actions. Huawei promised to open-source weights and training and inference code, but Pandaily reported no download location at publication. This is an announced AI development, without established deployment or independently verified superiority.

People building services with open-weight AI need requests to survive individual provider failures. Hugging Face now routes language-model requests through OpenRouter, selecting providers using live price, speed and reliability measurements and retrying failed requests elsewhere. OpenRouter says the integration currently offers one hundred sixty models from thirty-eight labs. Hugging Face says these requests now bill through its account, and users can no longer supply their own provider keys for those models.

Healthcare AI spending is moving beyond paperwork toward clinical support and patient interaction, according to Menlo Ventures. Its investor-produced report estimates clinical-copilot spending grew five and a half times to five hundred fifty million dollars, with AI models and agents supporting more complex workflows near patient care. Menlo estimates total healthcare-specific AI spending reached three point seven billion dollars. These are market estimates and survey findings, not proof of improved health outcomes or lower medical costs.

Health systems are using AI to investigate where services may need to expand. Definitive Healthcare’s conversational platform connects provider, claims and affiliation datasets; Bergen New Bridge Medical Center says it used the system to examine kidney-care and dialysis utilization. The company reports more than five hundred seventy analyses since its limited August launch and plans general availability in early twenty twenty-seven. The hospital’s reported analysis savings do not establish that care expanded or patient outcomes improved.

Young people facing barriers to employment are being offered practical AI training. OpenAI says its one-million-pound donation supports a partnership with The King’s Trust combining AI skills, recognized qualifications and employability support. The program aims to reach up to twenty-five thousand young people over eighteen months, prioritizing those outside education, employment or training. The wider qualifications program is still being developed, and employment outcomes remain prospective.

Connected workplace AI can act on business activity without waiting for a new request. OpenAI’s Holiday Extras case study says an employee’s assistant noticed an app launch, queried company data and delivered a performance report without being asked. Another employee reported analysis during his commute, and a colleague said an assistant animated existing three-dimensional app characters in about ten minutes. These are vendor-published employee accounts, rather than independently measured organization-wide productivity results.

Scientists are using ChatGPT to develop research ideas, beyond simply retrieving information. OpenAI analyzed more than five hundred eighty thousand scientific messages from one thousand eight hundred nineteen scientists in its summer pilot, and surveyed two hundred fifty-one participants. It reports sixty-eight percent of pilot scientists used ChatGPT to develop ideas. The study describes message activity and participant expectations; it does not establish faster or better discoveries.

AI-assisted scan review can help specialists identify suspected brain aneurysms while keeping physicians responsible for diagnosis. CINA-Aneurysm uses supervised deep learning to flag suspected saccular aneurysms larger than three millimeters on head CT angiography, supplying location and size. The FDA cleared it on October twenty, twenty twenty-six; the developers announced the clearance on November thirteen and were preparing United States commercialization. The software must not replace full patient evaluation or be relied on alone to confirm a diagnosis.

AI can flag students who need support, but those predictions miss personal circumstances that shape effective help. A study first submitted in May twenty twenty-five examined algorithm-assisted advising at Georgia State, distinguishing risk alerts from advisers’ knowledge of health, finances, schedules and engagement. The authors estimated two-thirds of interventions drew on context unavailable to the algorithm. Princeton’s current retrospective summary revisits that older research; the findings support human judgment alongside AI alerts, rather than demonstrating that AI alone improved graduation.

WILLIAM BLAIR CUT USA RARE EARTH $USAR. IT FELL 12.6%:

USA Rare Earth (USAR) at $7.13, -$1.03 / -12.62% on Monday.

USA Rare Earth is still on none of the Len5es we weigh, and on Monday William Blair downgraded it over a shortage of rare earth metals at its plants and the wait for Round Top, its Texas deposit, the two problems we wrote about on November 10. The fall erased a small gain since our post and left the shares at their lowest close since April 2025. Neal Dingmann, the William Blair analyst, moved the sales he expects from the company out into 2028. A fund of rare earth stocks fell less than half as far on Monday, but it had been losing ground since our post. The company's latest quarterly report says its federal funding agreements require it to raise more money by selling stock, and at a lower price each dollar takes more new shares. President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, China's president, meet this week with rare earth exports on the agenda, and USA Rare Earth blames China's export limits for its shortage.

USA Rare Earth is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es. Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying, and USA Rare Earth's last quarter brought in $3.0M. What would put it on the Hypergrowth Len5 is unchanged: sales that climb quarter after quarter once Serra Verde, the Brazilian mine it bought in September, starts adding to them. Momentum wants a stock near its high, and Monday's close sits 78.3% under June 3's high of $32.80. The business lost $141.4M from operations in the September quarter; an operating profit is the first thing the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 would need, and the Quality Len5 needs one too.

Monday took back everything USA Rare Earth had gained since our post.
- Friday's close: $8.16, 3.0% above the $7.92 in our post.
- Monday's open: $7.65, with about half the day's loss already in place.
- Monday's close: 2 cents above the day's low, and the lowest close since April 3, 2025.
- Since our post: -$0.79 / -10.0%.
The one-year low of $6.84, set during trading on November 5, still stands.

Dingmann cut his rating to market perform from outperform, William Blair's term for a stock it favors, and set no price target, Carl Surran of Seeking Alpha reported. Surran wrote that Dingmann pushed his estimates of USA Rare Earth's sales and profit margins out well into 2028, citing a shortage of raw materials at Less Common Metals, the British metals business, and so at the magnet plant in Stillwater, Oklahoma. Thras Moraitis, the chief executive, named the missing materials on November 9 as dysprosium oxide and samarium metal. Dingmann noted that everything Serra Verde produces in its first phase is committed for 15 years to a buyer set up with Pentagon money, and that help from Round Top is still years away, Surran wrote. Dingmann wrote that he favors "companies that have a longer history of processing material for the near term." We had the shortage and the Round Top delay on November 10. We had not tied Serra Verde's sold-out first phase to the magnet plant. USA Rare Earth's own target is finished magnet prototype sales to several customers from Stillwater by the end of 2026, the first dated check on Dingmann's point.

VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ETF (REMX) at $47.06, -$2.96 / -5.92% on Monday, a fund of rare earth and metals miners. MP Materials (MP) at $36.09, -$2.67 / -6.89% on Monday. Since our post, against USA Rare Earth's 10.0% loss:
- The fund: -3.5% through Friday, -9.2% through Monday.
- MP Materials: -1.0% through Monday.
David Moadel of 24/7 Wall St. wrote that the downgrade brought the group down, and that MP's softer decline fits its "standing as the group's established producer." Our read: the downgrade explains USA Rare Earth's extra loss on Monday, and the fund was falling before it. MP Materials is on none of those five Len5es; it has lost money in all three quarters of 2026.

USA Rare Earth's latest quarterly report says its funding agreements with the Commerce Department require it to raise additional equity, money from selling new shares or, for up to $300.0M, notes that convert into shares:
- By March 31, 2027: $375.0M, plus the cash costs of buying Serra Verde.
- By December 31, 2027: $875.0M.
For whatever part is still to raise, new shares needed for each $100M:
- At Monday's $7.13: about 14.0M, 3.7% of the 375.3M outstanding.
- At $17.85, the price at which it booked the shares it paid for Serra Verde: about 5.6M.
No Commerce money had been paid out by September 30.

USA Rare Earth stays off every Len5 we weigh, with an analyst's sales estimates moved into 2028 and equity deadlines in 2027. Trump and Xi are due to meet in Shenzhen at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on November 18-19, and the White House says the talks will take up China's compliance with rare earth export agreements, Ben Werschkul of Yahoo Finance reported. Our read: Rob Steele, the chief financial officer, blamed China's export limits for the shortage, so that meeting bears on the dysprosium and samarium its plants lack.

text:
$INTC @intel is building Noah’s Ark for American chip production.

The pain is front-loaded. From now through 2029 you are going to hear about cash burn, yield learning, timeline slips, and “why isn’t the foundry profitable yet?” That’s the nature of building leading-edge fabs. 

They are slow, brutally expensive, and take years of construction, tool installation, and process qualification before they become real capacity.

What is Intel actually building?:
•Arizona Fab 52 is already in high-volume production on 18A.
•Fab 62 has tools going in and is targeted for late 2028.
•Oregon remains the High-NA EUV development engine, with 14A high-volume targeted for 2028.
•Ireland is getting a ~$5.7B expansion of existing capacity for more Intel 3/Xeon server volume, majority of the spend by end-2027.
•Ohio’s first major fab is delayed but still moving toward 2030–2031 operations.
•Process progress is real, 18A in volume with improving yields/costs; 14A PDK 0.9 out, PDK 1.0 targeted early 2027, risk production H2 2027, high-volume 2028.

By 2030–2032 the picture flips. The heavy construction and process-qualification phase is largely behind them. Intel will control a large block of leading-edge capacity on US soil (plus meaningful volume in Ireland). In a world where almost everyone else is fabless and dependent on Taiwan, that is a scarce strategic asset, the closest thing the US has to a domestic Noah’s Ark for advanced chip production.

The market is pricing the 2026–2029 noise. The national-security and scarcity value of the capacity that emerges after that is what the long-term contrarian bet is actually about.

By 2032 Intel will be plus $500 and a National security asset with bi-partisan support.
